TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…
FILES: pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the DaemonSet controller marks pods as misscheduled based on node taints present at scheduling time but fails to re-evaluate and update the DaemonSet status when those taints disappear from the node later. This stale status happens due to missing triggers or watchers to detect node taint removals and update the DaemonSet status accordingly, causing persistent misscheduled reports even after the node becomes ready again.

No direct daemonset status update logic or taint watch is found in daemonset_util.go, suggesting the mechanism to update status on taint changes may be missing or incomplete.
The stale misscheduled status is caused by failure to trigger a status update upon node taint removal, as a manual label update triggers correct status refresh.

TITLE: Pods are stuck ContainerCreating after volume detach error and KCM restart
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

After KCM restart, any Pod that reuses a volume that failed to detach gets stuck ContainerCreating with message:

`
User "system:node:ip-10-0-243-205.us-east-2.compute.internal" cannot get resource "volumeattachments" in API group "storage.k8s.io" at the cluster scope: no relationship found between node 'ip-10-0-243-205.us-east-2.compute.internal' and this object
`

See steps to reproduce below, it's quite a complex condition. It happens when a pod is restarted, a CSI driver "busy" (i.e. times out) + KCM restarted at a wrong time.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pods start just fine.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


1. Create a Pod that uses an attachable CSI volume.
2. Delete the Pod. Make sure it unmounts successfully, but any `ControllerUnpublish` fails with a transient error, such as timeout. The external attacher continues to detach the volume at this point.
3. Stop kube-controller-manager (KCM) and start a new one. Wait for any leader election etc - it's important for the new KCM to populate A/D controller with no pod using the detaching volume. Let the A/D controller to observe detach error.
4. Create
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurs because after a failed detach attempt, the attach/detach controller incorrectly marks the volume as fully attached instead of uncertain. This causes Kubernetes to believe the volume is attached when it might still be detaching, leading to Pod mounting attempts on volumes that are not truly attached. Additionally, after KCM restart, volumes without Pods are marked as uncertain but also incorrectly as attached in the actual state of the node, which prevents proper re-attachment and causes Pods to get stuck during container creation.
FIX: Fixed attaching volumes after detach errors. Now volumes that failed to detach are not treated as attached, Kubernetes will make sure they are fully attached before they can be used by pods.
FILES: pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler_test.go, pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go

TITLE: Scheduler allows more volumes than a CSI driver limit to be attached
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a pod that uses an attachable volume is deleted, it can take some time for its volumes to get detached, but the scheduler does not care about it and treats Pod volumes as detached immediately after Pod is deleted from the API server.

The scheduler should count not only Pods, but also existing VolumeAttachment objects to get accurate nr. of volumes attached to the node.


### What did you expect to happen?

Scheduler respects the attachment limit and never puts more Pods with volumes when a CSI driver is still detaching a volume for a deleted pod.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Get a CSI driver that reports an attach limit. Using AWS EBS, it reports 26 max. attachments in its CSINode:
    ```yaml
    spec:
      drivers:
      - allocatable:
          count: 26
        name: ebs.csi.aws.com
    ```
2. Create many pods targeting the same node using a `nodeSelector`, each of them using its own AWS EBS PV.
3. See scheduler tries to schedule just 26 Pods on the node, the rest is Pending.
4. Delete one Running Pod. Once the Pod is deleted, the scheduler puts a new Pod to the node immediately. But
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler incorrectly counts attached volumes for scheduling by only considering volumes of existing pods, ignoring VolumeAttachment objects that persist briefly after pod deletion. This causes the scheduler to underestimate the number of volumes currently attached to a node, leading to overscheduling beyond the CSI driver's attachment limit.
FIX: scheduler: Improve CSILimits plugin accuracy by using VolumeAttachments
FILES: pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/csi.go, pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/csi_test.go, pkg/scheduler/testing/framework/fake_listers.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/testdata/cluster-roles.yaml

TITLE: In-tree vSphere volumes are not detached after KCM restart
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I am enabling CSI migration on a vSphere cluster. A node was fully drained, all its Pods are deleted, but just before KCM detaches in-tree vSphere volume volumes from it, KCM restarts. A new KCM starts, sees attached volumes in `node.status.volumesAttached` that are not needed by any Pod on the node and calls vSphere in-tree volume plugin `Detach()`.

The in-tree vSphere volume plugin + cloud provider marks the volume as detached right away, without reaching to vCenter API. The volume remains attached forever.

I don't think it's related to CSI migration, IMO a regular node drain + KCM restart at the same time can cause the same issue.

KCM logs:

```
I0404 14:58:42.423920       1 operation_generator.go:1637] Verified volume is safe to detach for volume "nil" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/vsphere-volume/[WorkloadDatastore] 8b577f5f-ea23-1e5e-bac9-0693938623e5/_029e/_0040/7f718f6c06a84cff86e254dfcd150be1.vmdk") on node "jsafrane-rdpmz-worker-ps6qk" 
I0404 14:58:42.423986       1 nodemanager.go:359] No VM found for node "jsafrane-rdpmz-worker-ps6qk". Initiating rediscovery.
E0404 14:58:42.434007       1 nodemanager.go:362] Error "No VM found" node info fo
ROOT CAUSE: The vSphere cloud provider maintains an internal cache of nodes using informer events that are asynchronous. During kube-controller-manager startup, this cache may not yet be fully populated when volume detach operations occur. As a result, the cloud provider cannot find the node in its cache, mistakenly assumes the volume is detached, and skips calling the vCenter API to detach the volume. This causes the volume to remain indefinitely attached in vCenter.
FIX: Fixed vSphere cloud provider not to skip detach volumes from nodes at kube-controller-startup.
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/legacy-cloud-providers/vsphere/nodemanager.go, staging/src/k8s.io/legacy-cloud-providers/vsphere/nodemanager_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/legacy-cloud-providers/vsphere/vsphere.go

TITLE: CSI volumes left overs are not cleaned up if CSI plugin is attachable
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

1. Create a Deployment or SS that uses a vsphere CSI volumes (for example).
2. Shutdown the node while pod was running.
3. Wait for node to go `NotReady` and pod to switch to `Terminating` state.

1. The volume types that are attachable, kubelet expects `node-publish-path` to be a mount point during reconstruction. So if node is rebooted then reconstruction fails because `/mount` path is not a mount point.
2. Kubelet tries to "Cleanup" the volume, but CSI driver may be unavailable at this point.
3. As a result volumes are never cleaned up.




### What did you expect to happen?

Expected cleanup to happen properly. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

master

### Cloud provider

Any

### OS version

Linux

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because kubelet incorrectly assumes that the volume's publish path is still a mount point during volume reconstruction after a node reboot. When the node is down and the path is no longer mounted, reconstruction fails, and kubelet attempts to clean up volumes without verifying mount existence, leading to failure in cleanup and persistent volume directories. The CSI driver being unavailable exacerbates the cleanup failure.

(#111933) Meanwhile Kubelet will print the log `Orphaned pod "xxx" found, but error not a directory occurred when trying to remove the volumes dir` every 2 seconds. (#105536)

TITLE: CSI migration race condition can cause unexpected detach and data loss
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

After the cluster was updated to enable PD CSI Driver, there was a race condition where AD Controller (kube-controller-manager) started to [populate the desired state of world](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc2898b20c6bd9602ae1c3b51333e2e4640ed249/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L438-L447) BEFORE the PD CSI Driver was up, thus AD Controller gave us the error 

```
Error creating spec for volume "elasticsearch", pod "XXX"/"elasticsearch-0": error performing CSI migration checks and translation for PVC "dXX"/"elasticsearch-elasticsearch-0": in-tree plugin kubernetes.io/gce-pd is migrated on node gke-stage-XXXXX but driver pd.csi.storage.gke.io is not installed.
```

Then AD Controller triggered the disk detach because the disk/volume was not populated in the desired state of world.

Unfortunately the disk was in use during this detach and got corrupted.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since cluster upgrades can cause the controller manager and CSI drivers to start at different times, the AD controller needs to be more conservative when detaching

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as 
ROOT CAUSE: The attach-detach (AD) controller initiated population of the desired state of the world before the CSI driver was fully up and running on the node. Because of this ordering issue (a race condition), the controller failed to recognize the CSI migrated volume properly and therefore triggered an erroneous detach operation on a volume still in use, leading to data corruption.
FIX: Fix an issue where a CSI migrated volume may be prematurely detached when the CSI driver is not running on the node.
If CSI migration is enabled on the node, even the csi-driver is not up and ready, we will still add this volume to DSW.
FILES: pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/util/util.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/util/util_test.go, pkg/volume/testing/volume_host.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because when a CSI volume's attach requirement changes from true to false, the attach/detach controller fails to mark the volume as "Uncertain" after a failure in MarkVolumeAsAttached. This causes the volume to be removed from the desired state of world (DSW) prematurely, leaving the associated VolumeAttachment object stranded and not cleaned up.

claims.text: The Attach function calls MarkVolumeAsAttached after successfully attaching the volume. If MarkVolumeAsAttached fails, the error is returned but the volume state is not marked as "Uncertain" to trigger retries later, potentially leaving the volume in a partially attached state.

TITLE: Kubernetes Jobs API rapid-fire scheduling doesnt honor exponential backoff characteristics
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

# Problem

The job controller appears to "rapidly reschedule" several pods at the same time (without backing off) which ultimately appears almost like a batch or gang scheduling workflow.  

... This is the opposite of what the job docs say, bc they clearly state :
```
 The back-off limit is set by default to 6. Failed Pods associated with the Job are recreated by the Job controller with an exponential back-off delay (10s, 20s, 40s ...) capped at six minutes.
```
So, rather then, 

- 10, 20, 40, 80 wait times between trying things we are seeing
- 0, 3, 3, 3, 3 second wait times before pods are being retried

This is in the 1.25 release, but not sure if it also happens earlier.  You can see this in the latest kind version. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Jobs wouldnt schedule the same pod at rapid fire intervals

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

# Details 

Thanks to Ryan for this reproducer: 
```
apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

  name: backoff-exp

spec:

  backoffLimit: 100

  template:

    spec:

      containers:

        - name: die

          image: ubuntu


ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller's back-off logic was coupled with the workqueue's back-off mechanism, causing rapid rescheduling of failed pods without proper exponential delay. This coupling meant multiple pod failures within a reconciliation cycle did not properly aggregate back-off delays, resulting in retries being scheduled too frequently and ignoring exponential backoff requirements.
FIX: The job controller back-off logic is now decoupled from workqueue. In case of parallelism > 1, if there are multiple new failures in a reconciliation cycle, all the failures are taken into account to compute the back-off. Previously, the back-off kicked in for all types of failures; with this change, only pod failures are taken into account. If the back-off limits exceeds, the job is marked as failed immediately; before this change, the job is marked as failed in the next back-off.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: kubelet: PreStop Hooks can hang termination of a pod beyond pod's termination grace period
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Termination grace period includes the termination time of prestop hooks and containers in the pod. The total time that the pod terminates should always be < termination grace period seconds.

TITLE: Named ports specified in sidecar container pod spec are not available to services
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When migrating a sidecar container to a native sidecar container (initContainer with restartPolicy=Always), traffic going via the Kubernetes Service did not reach the application container/sidecar container.

### What did you expect to happen?

The traffic should have reached the sidecar container like before the migration.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a Pod with a native sidecar container (initContainer) with a named port, as well as a Kubernetes Service using that named port as its targetPort. This port is not listed in the Endpoint.

Apply the following:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sidecar-ports
  labels:
    app: sidecar-ports
spec:
  containers:
  - image: bloomberg/goldpinger:3.10.1
    name: goldpinger
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
  initContainers:
  # note: no envoy configuration is provided, the steps to reproduce involve reading other Kubernetes manifests (Endpoints)
  - image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.73.7
    name: tls-terminator
    ports:
    - containerPort: 9443
      name: https
      protocol: TCP
--
ROOT CAUSE: The Kubernetes endpoint controller did not consider named ports declared in initContainers with restartPolicy=Always as available ports for Services endpoints. This omission caused Services targeting those named ports to not have corresponding ports listed in their Endpoints resource, preventing traffic from reaching the sidecar container through the Service.
FIX: The name port of the sidecar will also be allowed to be used

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…
FILES: pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

TITLE: NodePort will not listen on external IP if same IP is used as loadBalancerIP
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Hey, after upgrading kubernetes from 1.22 to 1.23, I'm experiencing strange service provisioning behavior using nodePort. I'm using kube-proxy (ipvs) + calico + metallb. 
If external IP is used by another service type (Loadbalancer - allocated by metallb), then the node owning this IP doesn't listen to NodePort on this interface.  
Unfortunately, I can't find any changes that could be causing this, any ideas?
Kubernetes 1.23
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  annotations:
    metallb.universe.tf/loadBalancerIPs: externalip1
  name: service
spec:
  ports:
  - name: client
    port: 31010
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: client
  type: LoadBalancer
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: service2
spec:
  ports:
  - appProtocol: http
    name: http
    nodePort: 32080
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: http
  - appProtocol: https
    name: https
    nodePort: 32443

```
``` console
ipvsadm -Ln | grep externalip1
node1:
    TCP  externalip1:31010 lc
    TCP  externalip1:32010 lc
node2:
    TCP  externalip1:31010 lc
ROOT CAUSE: In IPVS proxy mode, node IP addresses that were set as LoadBalancer IPs were also assigned to the kube-ipvs0 interface. Since NodePort services listen on all addresses except those assigned to kube-ipvs0, the NodePort ports on those node IPs that were also used as LoadBalancer IPs were excluded, causing the NodePort not to listen on those interfaces.

FILES: pkg/proxy/ipvs/netlink.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/netlink_linux.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/netlink_unsupported.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/testing/fake.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/testing/fake_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The root cause is that the node port scheduling plugin only accounts for host ports declared in the pod's main containers and completely omits ports specified in initContainers. Because initContainers can also request host ports (implicitly via hostNetwork or explicitly via hostPort), failure to consider their ports causes the scheduler to incorrectly allow pods with conflicting ports in their initContainers to be scheduled on the same node.

claims.text: The function getContainerPorts in pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodeports/node_ports.go explicitly only collects ports from pod.Spec.Containers, ignoring pod.Spec.InitContainers, causing initContainer ports to be omitted from node port conflict checks.

Because the host ports from initContainers are ignored, the scheduler does not detect conflicts when pods use the same hostPort in initContainers, leading to multiple pods being scheduled on the same node with conflicting ports.

Past experience with a similar omission of initContainers ports in other Kubernetes components (e.g., endpoint controller excluding named ports in initContainers) demonstrates the risk of omitting initContainer ports in port conflict or resource availability computations.

My setup is as follows:

* IMEX channels from the second pool are part of "IMEX domain 2" and can be attached to nodes 4-7

With this setup, I create two ResourceClaims, one ResourceClaim template, and 2 deployments. The two resource Claims are for two distinct IMEX channels, the ResourceClaimTemplate is for all GPUs on a given node, and the 2 deployments (of 4 replicas each) consume these claims / claimtemplates across each replica in order to simulate running 2 MPI jobs across two different IMEX domains.

Here are the specs:
```
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:

---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: shared-imex-channel0
spec:

    - name: channel
      deviceClassName: imex.nvidia.com
---
apiVersion: re
ROOT CAUSE: The allocationMode 'All' support in the structured dynamic resource allocator was incorrectly implemented, leading to incorrect device allocation that ignored device class selectors and failed to properly coordinate multiple claims. This caused the allocator to allocate devices that did not meet selector criteria or fail to find valid allocation solutions, resulting in pods remaining pending indefinitely.

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that when a Pod has its spec.nodeName field set (indicating it is pre-assigned to a specific node), the Dynamic Resources scheduler plugin is bypassed and does not run. Since this plugin is responsible for managing resource claims and reservations, bypassing it leads to the pod being rejected or failing to run because its resource claims are not properly allocated or reserved. This limitation arises because the scheduler plugin is skipped when the pod is pre-scheduled, preventing the dynamic resource allocation logic from executing.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller_test.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/controller_policy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/controller/controller.go, test/e2e/dra/dra.go, test/e2e/dra/test-driver/app/controller.go, test/integration/util/util.go

Specifically, when no devices are published on a node, the slice of allDevices is empty and numDevices is zero, but the allocation code does not contain an explicit check to fail allocation in this case. Past incidents concerning allocationMode All have shown the allocator logic was prone to errors in handling allDevices and device selectors; this indicates that the complex allocation logic requires explicit checks for empty device sets to uphold semantic correctness.

TITLE: Status of pods can become "OutOfCpu" when many pods are created and completed in a short time on the same node.
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Status of pods can become "OutOfCpu" when many pods are created and completed in a short time on the same node.

### What did you expect to happen?

Status of pods should become "Running", "Pending" or "Completed".

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I created a procedure to reproduce this state.
https://gist.github.com/shioshiota/84f1f4e162c335fe551c60a118676c3c

### Anything else we need to know?

We couldn't reproduce this behavior in kubernetes 1.21.2 cluster.
We found this issue in kubernetes 1.22.4.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"21", GitVersion:"v1.21.3", GitCommit:"ca643a4d1f7bfe34773c74f79527be4afd95bf39", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-07-15T21:04:39Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.6", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.4", GitCommit:"b695d79d4f967c403a96986f1750a35eb75e75f1", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-11-23T01:42:25Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.10", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/arm64"}
```

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>
no
</details>


ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Kubelet prematurely marked pods as terminated (Succeeded or Failed) in the API before all containers were fully stopped and prevented from restarting. This caused rapid repurposing of node resources and led to inaccurate 'OutOfCpu' errors on subsequent pods, due to resource accounting being inconsistent during quick pod turnover.
FIX: Fixed a 1.22 regression that could incorrectly reject pods with OutOfCpu errors if they were rapidly scheduled after other pods were reported as complete in the API. The Kubelet now waits to report the phase of a pod as terminal in the API until all running containers are guaranteed to have stopped and no new containers can be started.  Short-lived pods may take slightly longer (~1s) to report Succeeded or Failed after this change.

TITLE: Flag to Disable the 6-minute Force Detach Window
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Certain online upgrade workflows might need to restart kubernetes as a part of their upgrade procedure. This can lead to the following sequence:
* As a part of draining a kubernetes node, a pod might get deleted.
* The unmount of a pod could take more than 6 minutes.
* If the node is deemed unhealthy when the 6 minute timer fires for the pod being deleted (for example, because kubelet is still restarting), then the underlying PV will be force detached (via a `ControllerUnpublishVolume` RPC)

These workflows would likely benefit from disabling this feature in lieu of the Non-Graceful Node Shutdown feature that hit GA in kubernetes 1.28 (see [here](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/) for more details).

When these issues are encountered in our testbeds, we are left with Zombie iSCSI LUNs. If pods end up migrating to a node with such a Zombie LUN present, those pods might end up attaching themselves to the Zombie LUN leading to data corruption.

This data corruption has caused a number of our cluster-management applications to lose all access to their data, requiring them to be deployed from scratch (occasi
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurs because there is a built-in 6-minute timeout after which volumes are force detached if the node is unhealthy, regardless of whether the pod has successfully unmounted the volume. This force detachment can cause persistent volumes to become stuck in a 'Zombie' state, leading to data corruption when pods attach to these stale volumes. The root cause is the rigid 6-minute force detach window that triggers detach operations without accounting for longer unmount durations and node restart circumstances.
FIX: This change adds the following CLI option for `kube-controller-manager`:
* `disable-force-detach` (defaults to `false`): Prevent force detaching volumes based on maximum unmount time and node status. If enabled, the non-graceful node shutdown feature must be used to recover from node failure (see https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/). If enabled and a pod must be forcibly terminated at the risk of corruption, then the appropriate VolumeAttachment object (see here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/volume-attachment-v1/) must be deleted.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/options/attachdetachcontroller.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller_test.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/config/types.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/config/v1alpha1/zz_generated.conversion.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler_test.go, pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go, staging/src/k8s.io/kube-controller-manager/config/v1alpha1/types.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The kubectl exec sessions introduced in Kubernetes 1.30 default to using a WebSocket-based protocol for streaming command inputs and outputs. This WebSocket protocol has an idle timeout (around 5 minutes) that was not present in previous SPDY-based exec implementations, causing sessions to disconnect automatically after a fixed idle period. The disconnection happens because the WebSocket connection is closed server-side after this idle timeout, which the client observes as an instantaneous disconnect without errors.

claims.text: Starting in kubectl 1.30, exec commands were changed to use a WebSocket protocol for communication which introduced new idle timeouts not present before causing disconnections after approx 5 minutes of idleness.
Settting the environment variable KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS=false avoids the issue, indicating it is caused by the new WebSocket exec protocol default in 1.30.
This behavior was not observed in versions before 1.30 where SPDY was the default protocol for exec sessions, supporting longer or indefinite idle times without disconnects.
The issue was fixed in Kubernetes 1.30.4 which either changed the default behavior or fixed the idle timeout handling on WebSocket exec connections.

TITLE: Reflector retains initial list result for a long time
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The result of initial list in Reflector is kept in the memory until the last element in the items list hasn't been changed. 

In practice this can be a long time, e.g. there can be some stable pod that are running for days, in configmaps there is a kube-root-ca.crt which stays there forever.

This problem is described here: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro#a-possible-gotcha

IIUC this affects both:
* clients using informers/Reflectors
* kube-apiserver which is using the same Reflector to initialize watch cache

This means e.g. when all (but 1) elements are frequently updated, the memory usage is 2x the state size (the initial size + current size).

### What did you expect to happen?

When the objects are deleted from the cluster, the memory consumption of the Reflector drops.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create cluster with 1GB state of significant size (e.g. by creating 1000 configmaps of size 1M each)
* Start informer (e.g. I was using https://gist.github.com/mborsz/8964c84b298ee63c7153190d608a7464)
* Observe memory usage (it should be around ~1GB as expected)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-i
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the initial list result in the Reflector retains references to a large slice of objects, and if any object pointer from that slice is still in use, the Go runtime keeps the entire backing array in memory. This happens because the ObjectList contains a slice of objects (not pointers), and the Reflector takes pointers to these objects, preventing garbage collection of the initial slice. Thus, memory is not freed even when most objects are deleted or changed, leading to high memory consumption.
FIX: client-go: Improved memory use of reflector caches when watching large numbers of objects which do not change frequently
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta/help.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta/help_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/unstructured/unstructured.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/unstructured/unstructured_list.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/interfaces.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/testing/types.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/pager/pager.go

TITLE: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as po
ROOT CAUSE: The code for constructing REST requests accumulates errors internally but the URL() method ignores any existing errors and returns a URL regardless. This leads to users receiving misleading or incorrect URLs without an obvious indication that an earlier error occurred during request construction.
FIX: client-go: add an Error() function on Request
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request_test.go

TITLE: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and p
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cacher's readiness blocking mechanism was implemented using a sync.Cond variable that did not support context cancellation or timeouts. As a result, watch requests waiting for the cacher to become ready could be blocked indefinitely if the cacher was never marked ready, leading to infinite wait and resource exhaustion in concurrency queues.
FIX: cacher allow context cancellation if not ready
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cache_watcher_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher_whitebox_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/ready.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/ready_test.go

TITLE: client-go: the retry logic in rest.Request should be thread safe
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

the newly refactored retry logic introduced in 1.22 by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102217 broke the thread safety of `*Request`. According to Clayton, it's not a release blocker for 1.24. 
So the goal is to fix it in 1.25 and then back port all the way to 1.22.

Please note that there are other members (not related to retry logic) of `Request` that are not thread safe depending on how different methods of a `Request` object is used from multiple go routines.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102217/files#r837633535

Also, the comments on some of these methods and sections for retry logic can be improved:
- For instance, we may want to rename `IsErrorRetryable` to `IsHttpErrRetryable` and `checkWait` to `isServerIndicatedRetry`. 
That would have helped bring this back into mental cache faster and possibly help some future refactorer.


### What did you expect to happen?

Maintain thread safety of `*Request`
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the retry logic was refactored to use a retry interface as a member variable within the `Request` struct, which is not thread safe. This design allowed concurrent goroutines to share and modify the same retry state, violating the previous thread safety guarantees of the `Request` methods.
FIX: client-go: make retry in Request thread safe
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/with_retry.go

TITLE: Discovery memCacheClient has inconsistent error behavior with other DiscoveryInterfaces
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I think this got stale and closed because it was posted on `kubernetes/client-go` but is still very relevant:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/745

The [memCacheClient](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/f81a9405fae9d2a97f479bab1ab540fad1d2f178/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L47) created by memory.NewMemCacheClient(...) returns an error when calling ServerResourcesForGroupVersion if the APIResources list returned is empty, as seen here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/6d14209323d355841b67c4d9ca8c22fb1ca930a6/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L214-L216

Our particular case came up due to the `external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1` API group being registered with the API server, but having no resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

If using [NewMemcachedDiscoveryClient](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/cmd/root.go#L425) like [here](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/pkg/kubecfg/validate.go#L48) to discover `apiservices` with zero current resources there should not be an error returned.

### How can we reproduce i
ROOT CAUSE: The memCacheClient incorrectly treats an empty resource list in an API group version discovery response as an error, whereas other discovery clients do not. This causes spurious error logging when API groups exist but have no resources, such as aggregated metrics APIs. The root cause is that the memCacheClient implementation does not consistently handle empty resource lists as normal (non-error) responses.
FIX: Fixes a 1.26 regression in client-go discovery handling of empty responses
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because when the reflector encounters a watch decoding error caused by a client-side timeout, the underlying lengthDelimitedFrameReader masks the original timeout error and returns io.ErrShortBuffer instead. Consequently, this error does not satisfy the net.IsTimeout condition and is wrapped as an InternalError status event, which causes the reflector's retry logic to not retry the watch but instead trigger an expensive relist operation. This causes unnecessary relists on client timeouts instead of resuming the watch properly.

claims.text: The reflector's watch method triggers a relist operation when encountering InternalError by calling ShouldRetry, which returns false on the watch decoding error, causing a costly relist to happen on client timeouts.

The error returned by lengthDelimitedFrameReader masks the original timeout error as io.ErrShortBuffer, which leads to the watch error not being recognized as a timeout, causing the reflector to treat it as InternalError and not retry the watch.

TITLE: dynamic-resource-allocation: PrepareResource won't be called on node reboot
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We have k8s cluster with  Scalable function DRA driver deployed. 
We created Pod with resource claim to allocate Scalable function to Pod. 
When reboot the worker node the Pod with with Scalable function  failed to start with error [1].
The reason for the error is that PrepareResource is not called after reboot so we didn't create Scalable function  resource and prepare CDI file for it. 



[1] - Aug 09 09:58:45 cloud-dev-44 kubelet[1851]: E0809 09:58:45.873380    1851 remote_runtime.go:302] "CreateContainer in sandbox from runtime service failed" err="rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to create containerd container: CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices nvidia.com/net-sf=mlx5_core.sf.3" podSandboxID="5ce2a000bf64e9b7d9570a95e53718f9369376b866b22fbbeed22f8faca2c88b"
Aug 09 09:58:45 cloud-dev-44 kubelet[1851]: E0809 09:58:45.873586    1851 kuberuntime_manager.go:1212] container &Container{Name:ctr,Image:docker.io/busybox,Command:[sleep 10000],Args:[],WorkingDir:,Ports:[]ContainerPort{},Env:[]EnvVar{},Resources:ResourceRequirements{Limits:ResourceList{},Requests:ResourceList{},Claims:[]ResourceClaim{ResourceClaim{Name:sf,},},},VolumeM
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) manager incorrectly assumed that once a resource claim was prepared and cached, it remained valid even after a node reboot. FIX: DRA: call plugins for claims even if exist in cache

TITLE: `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` check blocks apiserver readiness for 1 minute if discovery cannot be completed
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

TITLE: CronJob gets stuck when jobs quota is reached
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We (in Booking.com) run CronJobs in Kubernetes clusters with ResourceQuota's defined. When quota for # of jobs is reached we observed that CronJobs:
1. stop scheduling new jobs (because quota is reached),
2. don't clean the old jobs (despite # of jobs > history allows and the fact that it would unblock the CronJob new Jobs). 

The only way to progress is to remove enough Jobs to make room for a new Job in namespace quota. When we do that manually, the CronJob kicks in.

The workaround we found around the internet is to specify `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` for the job template. But it's not ideal as it's not a history-based limit, but a time-based limit, and often you want to have the last N jobs to be around for debugging.

### What did you expect to happen?

When jobs quota is reached and # of cronjob jobs exceeds specified the history limit, these jobs are deleted giving room for new jobs to run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: job-quota
  namespace: default
spec:
  hard:
    count/jobs.batch: "1"
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metad
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because when the cronjob controller failed to create a new Job due to hitting the resource quota limit, it aborted the iteration early without performing cleanup of old finished Jobs. This prevented the controller from deleting obsolete Jobs to free quota, causing a deadlock where new Jobs could never be scheduled.
FIX: Fixed an issue where a CronJob could fail to clean up Jobs when the ResourceQuota for Jobs had been reached.

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The ResourceQuota controller computes the resource usage delta during an object's update by subtracting the previous usage from the new usage without accounting for changes in the object's quota scope memberships. When an object transitions from one scope to another (e.g., a Pod moving from NotTerminating to Terminating due to spec.activeDeadlineSeconds update), the delta calculation results in zero, causing no update to the associated quota usages. This stems from the logic in staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go where scope transitions are not considered in delta computation.

claims.text: The controller calculates delta usage for resource quota by simply subtracting previous object usage from current object usage without detecting a change in resource scopes during update events.

Because the controller ignores scope transitions, updating an object that changes scope results in a zero delta, so quota usage is not correctly adjusted for the new scope, causing stale or incorrect quota accounting.

We run kube-controller-manager as a static pod created by Kubelet and use the following command where we pass `--v=0`:
```

TITLE: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as po
ROOT CAUSE: The code for constructing REST requests accumulates errors internally but the URL() method ignores any existing errors and returns a URL regardless. This leads to users receiving misleading or incorrect URLs without an obvious indication that an earlier error occurred during request construction.
FIX: client-go: add an Error() function on Request

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

`kubectl logs POD_NAME -f ` won't output logs after kubelet rotate log filer of the container. 

### What did you expect to happen?

kubectl output logs correctly after the log file is rotated. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

2.  Build a image with this program
   ```
package main

 import (
        "fmt"
        "time"
 )

 func main() {
        i := 0
        for range time.Tick(10 * time.Microsecond) {
                fmt.Printf("print log to stand out %d\n", i)
                i++
        }
 }
   ```
3. Create a deploy with the previous image.
4. Run the command `kubectl logs POD_NAME -f`

_No response_

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"26", GitVersion:"v1.26.0", GitCommit:"b46a3f887ca979b1a5d14fd39cb1af43e7e5d12d", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-12-26T10:58:54Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

TITLE: cronjob controller: reconsider log verbosity
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running Kubernetes 1.25.5 and trying to configure kube-controller-manager to be less verbose when logging.
We run kube-controller-manager as a static pod created by Kubelet and use the following command where we pass `--v=0`:
```
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-controller-manager
    - --feature-gates=EphemeralContainers=true,TopologyAwareHints=true
    - --allocate-node-cidrs=true
    - --authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --authorization-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --cluster-cidr=10.6.0.0/16
    - --configure-cloud-routes=false
    - --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --leader-elect=true
    - --node-monitor-grace-period=120s
    - --root-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/ca.pem
    - --service-account-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/signing-key.pem
    - --use-service-account-credentials
    - --v=0
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.25.5
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    livenessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        host: 127.0.0.1
        path: /healthz
        po
ROOT CAUSE: The cronjob controller uses a global logging verbosity level of 3 for its event broadcaster, which is independent of the global -v flag passed to kube-controller-manager. As a result, event messages logged with verbosity 4 are always emitted if the global level is 3, ignoring the --v flag. This causes noisy logs even when low verbosity (e.g., --v=0) is requested. The root cause is the broadcaster's logging level is hardcoded and does not depend on the passed verbosity flag.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: increase the global level for broadcaster's logging to 3 so that users can ignore event messages by lowering the logging level. It reduces information noise.

TITLE: Status manager does not normalize ephemeral container statuses
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

`EphemeralContainerStatuses` is not normalized in 	`normalizeStatus()` in the status manager:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L1026-L1043

This does not seem to cause any user facing problem because `EphemeralContainerStatuses` is sorted before passed to the status manager and timestamps are normalized at marshaling to create a patch:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2336

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L873

However, an unexpected behavior is caused internally because timestamps are not normalized. If the log verbosity is 3 or larger, the following messages are logged periodically in kubelet when an ephemeral container exists:

```
May 14 20:10:33 kind-control-plane kubelet[720]: I0514 20:10:33.437155 	720 status_manager.go:230] "Syncing all statuses"
May 14 20:10:33 kind-control-plane kubelet[720]: I0514 20:10:33.438512 	720 status_manager.go:984] "Pod status is inconsistent with cache
ROOT CAUSE: The status manager failed to apply normalization logic to EphemeralContainerStatuses when processing pod status updates. This omission caused minor timestamp differences to persist, leading the kubelet to believe pod status was inconsistent and triggering continual unnecessary synchronization attempts.
FIX: normalize ephemeral container statuses

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Scheduler should use max(Spec.Resources.Requests, Status.Resources.Requests) instead of Status.AllocatedResources
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Current implementation of in-place pod resize looks at max(Spec.Resources, Status.Resources) which works well when resources are being increased, and works well when resources are being decreased assuming that the decrease request is based on observed lower usage, and the new lowered resources does not exceed current usage.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d86b74b0176c6fa22ba2559ace961fa25c6e98cf/pkg/api/v1/resource/helpers.go#L64-L73

However, a bad actor can game the system by requesting resize to resources lower than current usage, and kubelet grants it not knowing that runtime cannot enforce it, and scheduler may schedule pods to an oversubscribed node. A simple way to avoid this is to use Status.Resources.Requests instead of Status.AllocatedResources.

This also means that containerd and other runtimes need to be at a version that supports the feature so that users get the correct signals (avoid 'forever InProgress')


### What did you expect to happen?

When desired resources are lowered and kubelet admits it and sets status to InProgress, scheduler should schedule new pods against resources that are actually available. Bad actors sho
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler made scheduling decisions based on the max of requested and status resources without considering that the kubelet might have admitted a decrease below current actual usage. This allowed pods to be resized to resource amounts lower than what the runtime could enforce, causing potential oversubscription and incorrect scheduling.
FIX: ContainerStatus.AllocatedResources is now guarded by a separate feature gate, InPlacePodVerticalSaclingAllocatedStatus
FILES: pkg/api/pod/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util_test.go, pkg/features/kube_features.go, pkg/features/versioned_kube_features.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/helpers_linux.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/quota/v1/evaluator/core/pods.go, pkg/quota/v1/evaluator/core/pods_test.go

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` is enabled and only a memory resource request is configured in a pod, the minimum CPU request set internally is displayed in the pod status:
```
$ kubectl get pod testpod -o jsonpath='spec: {.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\nallocatedResources: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].allocatedResources}{"\nstatus: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].resources}{"\n"}'
spec: {"requests":{"memory":"200Mi"}}
allocatedResources: {"memory":"200Mi"}
status: {"requests":{"cpu":"2m","memory":"200Mi"}}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The minimum CPU request is not displayed in the pod status.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enables the `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` feature.
2. Create a pod where only memory request is configured:
   <Details>

   ```
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod
   metadata:
     labels:
       run: testpod
     name: testpod
   spec:
     containers:
     - image: nginx
       name: testpod
       resources:
         requests:
           memory: 200Mi
     restartPolicy: Always
   ```

   </Details>
3. See its resources in the pod status:
   ```
   $ ku
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happens because the Kubelet enforces a minimum CPU shares value (2m CPU) on Linux when the requested CPU resource is below that threshold or not specified. This leads to the pod status showing a minimum CPU request that was not originally specified in the pod spec, causing confusion and mismatch in resource reporting when only memory requests are configured.

TITLE: Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled:
```
E1127 19:48:13.221979   66549 schedule_one.go:130] "Error selecting node for pod" err="applying score defaultWeights on Score plugins: plugin \"PodTopologySpread\" returns an invalid score 300, it should in the range of [0, 100] after normalizing" pod="default/test-multi-point-xxxxxxxx"
```

After investigation, I found that there was a bug in the code that built the framework when the scheduler started. When using the plugins declared in the regular extension point to override the plugins declared in the MultiPoint, the traversed variable `enabledSet` will be modified in the following loop:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L523-L534

This may cause **a same scoring plugin** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`) **to be loaded multiple times**:
```
f.scorePlugins: []framework.ScorePlugin{(*noderesources.Fit)(0xc000922e10), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*tai
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the scheduler framework's logic to build plugin lists when merging MultiPoint plugins and regular plugins had a flaw in a loop that led to the same scoring plugin being included multiple times. This caused plugins like PodTopologySpread to execute NormalizeScore multiple times on the same node, producing invalid scores outside the expected [0, 100] range.
FIX: Fixed a regression since 1.24 in the scheduling framework when overriding MultiPoint plugins (e.g. default plugins).
The incorrect loop logic might lead to a plugin being loaded multiple times, consequently preventing any Pod from being scheduled, which is unexpected.

When reboot the worker node the Pod with with Scalable function  failed to start with error [1].
The reason for the error is that PrepareResource is not called after reboot so we didn't create Scalable function  resource and prepare CDI file for it. 



[1] - Aug 09 09:58:45 cloud-dev-44 kubelet[1851]: E0809 09:58:45.873380    1851 remote_runtime.go:302] "CreateContainer in sandbox from runtime service failed" err="rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to create containerd container: CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices nvidia.com/net-sf=mlx5_core.sf.3" podSandboxID="5ce2a000bf64e9b7d9570a95e53718f9369376b866b22fbbeed22f8faca2c88b"

TITLE: [SidecarContainers] Scheduler accounting sidecar resource requests as initContainers
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

As per [Sidecars KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/753-sidecar-containers/README.md#resources-calculation-for-scheduling-and-pod-admission), resources calculations for scheduling pods with sidecars is : Max ( Max( each InitContainerUse ) , Sum(Sidecar Containers) + Sum(Containers) ), but [scheduler logic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2d31ec00273c34390ec77637fb4ff96234885bca/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L950-L951) is using Max(RegularContainers, InitContainers) to calculate resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

Resource Requests = Max ( Max( each InitContainerUse ) , Sum(Sidecar Containers) + Sum(Containers) )

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2d31ec00273c34390ec77637fb4ff96234885bca/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L950-L951

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# paste output here
```

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>

</details>

### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
# pas
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's resource calculation logic incorrectly accounted sidecar container resource requests by only comparing max resource demands between init and regular containers, ignoring the summed resource requests of sidecar and regular containers together as required. This discrepancy caused underestimation of resource usage for pods with sidecars, violating the resource calculation formula defined in the Sidecars KEP.
FIX: Scheduler will start considering the resource requests of existing sidecar containers during the scoring process.
FILES: pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/fit_test.go, pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go, pkg/scheduler/framework/types_test.go, pkg/scheduler/testing/wrappers.go, pkg/scheduler/util/pod_resources.go, pkg/scheduler/util/pod_resources_test.go, test/e2e/scheduling/priorities.go, test/integration/scheduler/scoring/priorities_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug arises because the NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation plugin's method calculateResourceAllocatableRequest treats native resources (cpu and memory) differently from extended scalar resources by always accounting for node's requested resources regardless of the pod's actual requests. Specifically, when podRequest is zero for cpu or memory, it still returns the node's requested resources for scoring, causing different scores on nodes with differing resource usage. This deviates from the behavior for extended resources and results in skewed scheduling that concentrates pods with zero resource requests on certain nodes.

claims.text: The function calculateResourceAllocatableRequest returns (0,0) to bypass scoring for extended scalar resources when podRequest is zero, but for cpu and memory it returns the node's requested resources even if podRequest is zero, causing a difference in node scores for pods with no requests.

The code in utils.go uses IsPrefixedNativeResource to ignore extended resources but treats native resources like cpu and memory differently, indicating inconsistent handling of resources that leads to incorrect scoring.

TITLE: Termination signals not sent to Native Sidecars when multiple Native Sidecars
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In a situation where during the init phase of a `Pod`, a native sidecar never becomes ready (because its `startupProbe` is failing), then the `Pod` is terminated, if there are multiple startup containers, a termination signal is never received by the init container and the Pod is stuck (until `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is hit).

### What did you expect to happen?

All running initContainer to receive the termination signal correctly.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a `Dockerfile` with this bash script as an entrypoint:

```
#!/bin/bash
set -e 
trap 'echo "saw an exit signal"; sleep 5; exit' EXIT

while true; do
  echo "hello"
  sleep 1
done
```

Create a deployment with two init containers (one normal one sidecar).  Add an probe which means the startupProbe never passes

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: karl-test-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app2: karl-test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app2: karl-test 
    spec:
      securityContext:
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefaul
ROOT CAUSE: The termination logic failed to send termination signals to restartable init containers when some other restartable init containers had not yet started. This caused pods with multiple native sidecars to block termination signals if one sidecar never became ready during initialization, leaving the pod stuck without proper cleanup.
FIX: Fixed a bug that init containers with `Always` restartPolicy may not terminate gracefully if the pod hasn't initialized yet.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_termination_order.go, test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The kubelet fails to properly detect pod initialization phase after a node reboot when the pod has init containers with restartPolicy set to 'Always'. This occurs because container statuses alone do not reliably indicate the current pod sandbox state, causing the kubelet to mistakenly advance pod phase from pending to running without ensuring init containers have completed. The underlying defect arises from missing or insufficient tracking of pod sandbox identity (podSandboxID) in container status, leading to incorrect phase transitions after sandbox recreation during node reboot.

claims.text: The issue is that after a node reboot, the pod sandbox is recreated but the kubelet relies on container statuses to determine pod phase and initialization status, which is unreliable without associating container statuses to the current pod sandbox identity.

The suggestion was made to add podSandboxID to container.Status to reliably identify whether container statuses belong to the current pod sandbox. This indicates the root cause is missing correlation between container status and the active pod sandbox after reboot.

An e2e test updated at commit 65afe520 on the Kubernetes repo tries to reproduce the issue by removing the pod from container runtime and checking if pod remains in pending phase until re-initialized, but it fails because the pod transitions to Running prematurely, showing the phase determination logic is flawed.

The presence of related past bug kb-122902 shows that restartPolicy 'Always' on init containers can cause state transition logic issues, though that bug was about restart policy handling in readiness state, indicating complexity in handling restartable init containers' states.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the scheduler has a race condition involving the clearing of a pod's nominated_node_name when a higher priority pod fails scheduling and enters backoff. Specifically, if the re-addition of a low priority pod happens before the nominated_node_name of a medium priority pod is cleared (which happens asynchronously during its retry schedule after backoff), the scheduler erroneously thinks node resources are insufficient, causing the low priority pod to be unschedulable and significantly delaying its scheduling.

claims.text: The scheduling lifecycle involves asynchronous binding and scheduling cycles where pods are scheduled in order, and failed scheduling leads to retries after backoff.
When scheduling fails, a pod's nominated_node_name is cleared during the retry scheduling cycle to allow other pods to be scheduled without incorrect resource reservations.
The race condition occurs because the clearing of the nominated_node_name for a pod happens asynchronously during its retry schedule after backoff delay.

If a lower priority pod is re-added before the nominated_node_name of a higher priority pod is cleared, the scheduler incorrectly considers resources insufficient due to the still-set nomination, causing the lower priority pod to remain unschedulable for an extended period.
Adding a 2 second delay before re-adding the pod allows the nominated_node_name clearing to complete, preventing the race and resulting in proper scheduling.

3. Observe that there are two pods running.

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

TITLE: CronJob gets stuck when jobs quota is reached
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We (in Booking.com) run CronJobs in Kubernetes clusters with ResourceQuota's defined. When quota for # of jobs is reached we observed that CronJobs:
1. stop scheduling new jobs (because quota is reached),
2. don't clean the old jobs (despite # of jobs > history allows and the fact that it would unblock the CronJob new Jobs). 

The only way to progress is to remove enough Jobs to make room for a new Job in namespace quota. When we do that manually, the CronJob kicks in.

The workaround we found around the internet is to specify `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` for the job template. But it's not ideal as it's not a history-based limit, but a time-based limit, and often you want to have the last N jobs to be around for debugging.

### What did you expect to happen?

When jobs quota is reached and # of cronjob jobs exceeds specified the history limit, these jobs are deleted giving room for new jobs to run.

kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:

spec:
  hard:

---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metad

TITLE: A Job might finish with ready!=0, terminating!=0
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Job is declared Failed, the running Pods still count as ready.
This causes problems for higher level controllers that use the Failed/Completed conditions to do usage accounting. If the job is marked as finished before all the pods finish, the accounting is inaccurate.

TITLE: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a
