TITLE: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Currently kube-proxy efficiently cleans all stale conntrack entries preventing traffic black holing for deleted endpoints, but there can be some corner cases when conntrack cleaning happens before programming the network leaving a small window in which if any packet arrives will back-hole the traffic.

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:
1.  First one with EndpointConditions.Ready as false
2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the conntrack cleaning logic considers endpoint readiness changes as an indication to clean stale connections before the network datapath has been updated to reflect those changes. This causes a timing window where conntrack entries are cleaned ahead of actual network programming, potentially blackholing traffic.
FIX: Fix stale conntrack flow detection logic
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier_test.go, pkg/proxy/types.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the updateLoadBalancer function employs a caching mechanism keyed by a hash of the endpoints to avoid redundant updates. When endpoints change (e.g., scaling pods), the new hash differs, but the function may incorrectly detect the existing load balancer in the previousLoadBalancers map and return it as-is, without propagating the updated endpoint list to HNS. This prevents the HNS load balancer policy from being updated with the new endpoints after ModifyLoadBalancer API invocation.

claims.text: The updateLoadBalancer method uses a hash of endpoints to identify load balancers and caches them in a map previousLoadBalancers, returning early if a cached entry exists for the same hash, which can skip updates.

Due to this caching, when endpoints change and the hash changes, the function may still return a cached load balancer without updating endpoints in HNS, causing the endpoint list to remain stale after scaling pods.

TITLE: Graceful node shutdown doesn't wait for volume teardown
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We have observed that after a node is preempted, pods using persistent volumes take 6+ minutes to restart. This happens when a volume was not able to be cleanly unmounted (indicated by updating `Node.Status.VolumesInUse`), which causes the Attach/Detach controller (in kube-controller-manager) to wait for 6 minutes before issuing a force detach. In addition to a long pod restart period, an unclean mount could also cause data corruption.

From the logs we've observed the following non-ideal behaviors, which I think reduces to the same issue that we only check for containers' being terminated and not their volumes.

1. The CSI driver running on the node gets terminated before the workload's volumes get unmounted. This causes unmount to fail. In our case, the CSI driver is part of the `system-node-critical" class, but since we don't wait for volumes to be unmounted, we move on to shutting down the critical pods.

3. The OS gets shutdown before volume teardown is completed, even if there is still time left in the `shutdownGracePeriod`. In our case, the `shutdownGracePeriod` is set to 30 seconds, however we see that the node got shutdown in 10 seconds, even wh
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that during node shutdown, the shutdown manager checks only for pod termination to proceed without ensuring that volumes used by these pods are successfully unmounted. Since volume teardown only starts after containers have stopped, there is a race condition where the CSI driver may be terminated or the OS may shut down before volumes are fully detached, leading to unclean unmounts and prolonged pod restarts.
FIX: Node shutdown controller now makes a best effort to wait for CSI Drivers to complete the volume teardown process according to the pod priority groups.

TITLE: API: ResourceRequirements usage in Container and PVC
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The same ResourceRequirements struct is used in two only loosely related entities (Container and PersistentVolumeClaim). Extending ResourceRequirements for dynamic resource requirement had the unintended effect that the new `Claims` field also became available in a PersistentVolumeClaim.



### What did you expect to happen?

Extending one should not affect the other.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111023#pullrequestreview-1302112278:

> We just ran across this while reviewing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107776
>
> The ResourceRequirements type is also used within the PersistentVolumeSpec type (which is also used indirectly in pod specs via ephemeral volumes), and the "clear if feature-gate is disabled" logic is only wired to podspec-handling. That means in 1.26 PVC objects or PodSpecs with ephemeral volumes defined can persist data in this field even if the feature is disabled.
>
> Can you open a PR to clear this field in PVC and ephemeral volume create/update flows, and file a follow-up issue to consider splitting the type used in PVCs so it doesn't continue inheriting work done that is targeted at pods?

TOD
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the API design used the same ResourceRequirements struct for both Container and PersistentVolumeClaim entities. When the struct was extended to include a new Claims field for dynamic resource requirements targeting containers, this change also inadvertently affected PersistentVolumeClaim API, where the field was not applicable. This happened because the types were shared rather than having distinct resource requirement types for containers and volume claims, causing cross-impact due to type reuse.
FIX: Go API: the ResourceRequirements struct needs to be replaced with VolumeResourceRequirements for use with volumes.

TITLE: NodeExpandVolume gets called, even if CSI plugin returned NodeExpansionRequired=false in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

### What did you expect to happen?

The issue is seen with vSphere CSI driver, while expanding vSphere raw-block volume (volumeMode: Block), 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the kubelet does not respect the NodeExpansionRequired=false flag returned by CSI plugins in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse and still calls the NodeExpandVolume API unnecessarily. TITLE: Transient Driver Registration on the CSINode can Result in Missed NodeUnstageVolume RPCs During Pod Migration
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In `unmountDetachDevices` (see [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconciler_common.go#L279-L316)) we have the following code that will ultimately dispatch `NodeUnstageVolume` RPCs to the underlying CSI plugin.

Here is a pseudo-code representation of the current logic:

```
function unmountDetachDevices
	for all unmounted volumes in ASoW
		if volume not in DSoW &&
		   not operation pending on volume
			if device is mounted globally or
			   device is mounted uncertain
				Case A:
				unmount device
				(this will kick off the NodeUnstageVolume RPC; we want to be here)
			else
				Case B:
				just remove volume from ASoW
				(general badness since we don't issue a NodeUnstageVolume RPC)
```

In our testbeds, we have observed a number of occurrences where we fall into `Case B` when the CSI Node plugin for a particular driver is being bounced, which leads to the volumemanager failing to dispatch the `NodeUnstageVolume` RPC. If the pod migrates to another node, this will leave behind a Zombie LUN in our testbeds (we're using iSCSI).

A Zombie LUN can and often does resu
ROOT CAUSE: The CSI attacher treats the absence of the CSI driver during a NodeStageVolume call as a final error, transitioning volume devices from uncertain to unmounted state prematurely. This causes unmountDetachDevices logic to skip issuing NodeUnstageVolume RPCs, potentially leaving volumes in a zombie state. The root cause is misclassification of a missing CSI driver error as final rather than transient, leading to incorrect device state transitions and missed cleanup calls.
FIX: Retry NodeStageVolume calls if CSI node driver is not running

Although the volume is already resized on the controller side and the NodeExpansionRequired flag is false, this error is never cleared since the existing workaround for this scenario is only present in legacyCallNodeExpandOnPlugin, not in expandOnPlugin, leading to persistent misleading error status.

claims.text: The expandOnPlugin function in node_expander.go treats the lack of NodeExpandVolume support from the CSI driver as an error and sets the NodeResizeError condition, without handling operation-not-supported errors gracefully.

The existing workaround for handling operation-not-supported errors when NodeExpandVolume is unsupported exists in legacyCallNodeExpandOnPlugin but is missing in expandOnPlugin, causing persistent error conditions despite successful controller-side volume expansion.

The CSI driver sets NodeExpansionRequired=false in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse, indicating node expansion is not needed, but kubelet still attempts node expansion and reports errors due to missing support, consistent with previous known issues about ignoring this flag.

TITLE: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Currently kube-proxy efficiently cleans all stale conntrack entries preventing traffic black holing for deleted endpoints, but there can be some corner cases when conntrack cleaning happens before programming the network leaving a small window in which if any packet arrives will back-hole the traffic.

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:
1.  First one with EndpointConditions.Ready as false
2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the conntrack cleaning logic considers endpoint readiness changes as an indication to clean stale connections before the network datapath has been updated to reflect those changes. This causes a timing window where conntrack entries are cleaned ahead of actual network programming, potentially blackholing traffic.
FIX: Fix stale conntrack flow detection logic
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier_test.go, pkg/proxy/types.go

TITLE: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue
ROOT CAUSE: The kube-proxy component lacked a properly configured --nodeport-addresses setting in a dual-stack environment, causing it to listen on all IP interfaces (0.0.0.0 and ::) by default. This results in healthCheckNodePort binding to all zeros (wildcard address) instead of a node's specific IP, because the code defaults to listening on all addresses if no specific nodeport address ranges are configured.
FIX: The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)
FILES: cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_linux.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_test.go, pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/types.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation_test.go, pkg/proxy/apis/config/zz_generated.deepcopy.go, pkg/proxy/healthcheck/healthcheck_test.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go

This causes kube-proxy to fail in removing or overwriting the stale remote HNS endpoints, leading to conflicts and failures in creating the new Windows pod HNS endpoints with reused IP addresses.

claims.text: The issue involves HNS endpoint creation failure when Windows pods get assigned the same IP address as a previously deleted Linux pod, indicating that the logic handling Windows HNS endpoint management and IP reuse is flawed.

Similar past incidents and analysis suggest that kube-proxy’s Windows proxier code does not properly clean up or reconcile existing remote endpoints before creating new local endpoints, causing a conflict when IPs are reused.

TITLE: Job controller reports the count of ready pods with unnecessary delay
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When Job controller is deleting pods the counter in the status.ready field does not reflect this properly (there is a delay until the cache is refreshed). This affects the scenarios of terminating job, suspended job, and excess pods deleted.

### What did you expect to happen?

The ready field is updated as soon as the delete requests are sent successfully, in sync with the status.active field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. To see this you can scale down a job, use the following yaml:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: simple-job
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: 'worker'
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import time
          time.sleep(300)
```

2. Watch for the job updates with the following watcher:
```
kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,READY:.object.status.ready,ACTIVE:.object.status.active,TERMINATING:.object.status.terminat
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Job controller counts ready pods only among the currently active pods during deletion, but since the number of active pods updates asynchronously and may decrease after the count was made, the ready pod count does not get updated promptly to reflect pods that are terminating or deleted. This lag causes stale ready counts until the cache refreshes.
FIX: Now the .status.ready field is tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: The event handlers of job controller are slow
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The event handlers in job controller are much slower than other controllers. It can cause the ring buffer in the processorListener to grow unbounded when the job churn is high enough.
The processing logic in the job controller events handler appears to be more complicated than other controllers. e.g. in [updateJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L464-L504), it invokes function `cleanupPodFinalizers` that lists the pods matching some selectors and the enqueue them to another queue. Similarly in [deleteJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L508-L524).

I added some instrumenting code to understand the latency of each event handler.
For job controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.080 ms
job update event handler: 3.075 ms
job delete event handler: 3.076 ms
pod add event handler: 0.136 ms
pod update event handler: 0.709 ms
pod delete event handler: 0.405 ms

For ttl-after-completion controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.0065 ms
job update event handler: 0.024 ms

T
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the slowness is that the job controller's event handlers perform complex and expensive operations directly within the event handler methods, such as listing pods and enqueuing them, instead of deferring such processing to the controller's main reconcile loop. This design leads to high latency and potential buildup of events, especially under high job churn.
FIX: Improve performance of the job controller when handling job update events.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an intern
ROOT CAUSE: The job controller initiates creation of replacement pods immediately upon noticing a pod deletion without waiting for the original pod to fully terminate. This premature creation can lead to multiple pods running concurrently when parallelism is set to 1, violating users' expectations and causing application failures. The controller did not implement a mechanism to delay pod creation until the pod state was confirmed as terminated.
FIX: Add implementation for PodRecreationPolicy to wait for creation of pods once the existing ones are fully terminated.
FILES: pkg/controller/controller_utils.go, pkg/controller/controller_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: A Job might finish with ready!=0, terminating!=0
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Job is declared Failed, the running Pods still count as ready.
This causes problems for higher level controllers that use the Failed/Completed conditions to do usage accounting. If the job is marked as finished before all the pods finish, the accounting is inaccurate.

### What did you expect to happen?

A few options (non-necessarily exclusive), in order of my preference:
1. The job not to be declared Completed/Failed until all the Pods have finished. This is possibly a breaking change. As a mitigation, we can use the `FailureTarget` or `SuccessCriteriaMet` conditions to provide early feedback to controllers that a Job is marked for failure.
2. ~Do not count Pods with a deletionTimestamp as ready. (Possibly a breaking change)~
3. ~We just consider ready=0 if setting a finished condition~
4. Continue syncing a Job even after the Failed condition is added, until ready/terminating fields are zero.

Options 2 and 3 don't satisfy the requirement of proper accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Use this Job (note backoffLimit: 0):
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: inde
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the Job was marked as Failed or Completed as soon as failure or success conditions were met, without waiting for all Pods to reach a terminal state. This caused running Pods to still be counted as ready, leading to inaccurate accounting in higher-level controllers that rely on Job conditions.
FIX: Delay setting terminal Job conditions until all pods are terminal.

Additionally, the FailureTarget condition is also added to the Job object in the first Job
status update as soon as the failure conditions are met (backoffLimit is exceeded, maxFailedIndexes, 
or activeDeadlineSeconds is exceeded).

Similarly, the SuccessCriteriaMet condition is added in the first update as soon as the expected number
of pod completions is reached.

Also, introduce the following validation rules for Job status when JobManagedBy is enabled:
1. the count of ready pods is less or equal than active
2. when transitioning to terminal phase for Job, the number of terminating pods is 0
3. terminal Job conditions (Failed and Complete) should be preceded by adding the corresponding interim conditions: FailureTarget and SuccessCriteriaMet
FILES: pkg/apis/batch/validation/validation.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, pkg/controller/job/success_policy.go, pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy.go, pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy_test.go, test/e2e/apps/job.go, test/e2e/framework/job/wait.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: Job controller reports the count of terminating pods with unnecessary delay
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When Job controller is terminating and deletes all pods the counter in the `status.terminating` field does not reflect this properly. 

### What did you expect to happen?

The counter for the terminating pods is updated as soon as Job controller has this information. Similarly as for the counter of active pods.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

0. watch the job & pod updates with the commands:
`kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,STATUS:.object.status | ts "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%.S"`
`kubectl get pods -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,PHASE:.object.status.phase,FINALIZERS:.object.metadata.finalizers,DELETION:object.metadata.deletionTimestamp,CONTAINERS:.object.status.containerStatuses | ts "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%.S"`
1. Run the Job:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: indexed-job
  labels:
    jobgroup: indexedjob
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  backoffLimit: 0
  completionMode: Indexed
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
    
ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller failed to increment the counter for terminating pods when it actively deletes pods during job termination, particularly for failed jobs. This caused the .status.terminating field to not reflect terminating pods accurately, leading to delayed or incorrect status updates.
FIX: .status.terminating field now gets tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug arises because the job controller updates the job status fields related to succeeded pod counts and pod finalizers in the same reconcile loop iteration. This leads to a race when the watch event for the uncountedTerminatedPods status update is delayed under load, causing the controller to miscount succeeded pods and prematurely remove pod finalizers, thus creating multiple pods despite parallelism=1.

claims.text: The syncJob function processes Job.status.succeeded, pod finalizer presence, and Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods together in the same reconcile loop, causing possible miscounting when events are delayed.

The ticket describes that refreshing finalizer presence and uncountedTerminatedPods in the same sync leads to race conditions causing extra pods to be created when the watch event for uncountedTerminatedPods is delayed, especially in busy clusters.

Past incidents show that the job controller's pod counting and finalizer handling are sensitive to timing and ordering of updates, e.g., delayed status updates and immediate replacements of pods lead to similar correctness issues ([kb-125185], [kb-115844], [kb-123775], [kb-125089]).

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that when a Pod has its spec.nodeName field set (indicating it is pre-assigned to a specific node), the Dynamic Resources scheduler plugin is bypassed and does not run. Since this plugin is responsible for managing resource claims and reservations, bypassing it leads to the pod being rejected or failing to run because its resource claims are not properly allocated or reserved. This limitation arises because the scheduler plugin is skipped when the pod is pre-scheduled, preventing the dynamic resource allocation logic from executing.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller_test.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/controller_policy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/controller/controller.go, test/e2e/dra/dra.go, test/e2e/dra/test-driver/app/controller.go, test/integration/util/util.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the kubelet's Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) logic assumes that if it tried to prepare dynamic resources for a pod, then it always invoked NodePrepareResources successfully. However, it does not track whether NodePrepareResources actually succeeded before attempting to call NodeUnprepareResources during pod deletion. Consequently, if NodePrepareResources never completed (such as when the dynamic resource driver is missing), the kubelet incorrectly blocks pod deletion waiting for an unprepare call, causing the deletion to hang.

claims.text: The kubelet tries to unprepare resources assuming that NodePrepareResources was called successfully, but it does not track the actual success state of NodePrepareResources, leading to improper blocking on pod deletion when preparation never succeeded.

Past experience shows that failures in resource preparation are related to driver availability issues (plugin not found); the kubelet erroneously tries to unprepare resources regardless of whether preparation succeeded, leading to pod deletion delays.

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…
FILES: pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

TITLE: Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled:
```
E1127 19:48:13.221979   66549 schedule_one.go:130] "Error selecting node for pod" err="applying score defaultWeights on Score plugins: plugin \"PodTopologySpread\" returns an invalid score 300, it should in the range of [0, 100] after normalizing" pod="default/test-multi-point-xxxxxxxx"
```

After investigation, I found that there was a bug in the code that built the framework when the scheduler started. When using the plugins declared in the regular extension point to override the plugins declared in the MultiPoint, the traversed variable `enabledSet` will be modified in the following loop:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L523-L534

This may cause **a same scoring plugin** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`) **to be loaded multiple times**:
```
f.scorePlugins: []framework.ScorePlugin{(*noderesources.Fit)(0xc000922e10), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*tai
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the scheduler framework's logic to build plugin lists when merging MultiPoint plugins and regular plugins had a flaw in a loop that led to the same scoring plugin being included multiple times. This caused plugins like PodTopologySpread to execute NormalizeScore multiple times on the same node, producing invalid scores outside the expected [0, 100] range.
FIX: Fixed a regression since 1.24 in the scheduling framework when overriding MultiPoint plugins (e.g. default plugins).
The incorrect loop logic might lead to a plugin being loaded multiple times, consequently preventing any Pod from being scheduled, which is unexpected.

TITLE: scheduler: move all preCheck to QueueingHint
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In our custom plugin, we want to move pods that is unscheduled by the plugin to activeQ/backoffQ when a new Pod is created.
So, we define `EventsToRegister` like this:

```go
func (p *Plugin) EventsToRegister() []framework.ClusterEvent {
	return []framework.ClusterEvent{{
		Resource:   framework.Node,
		ActionType: framework.All,
	}, {
		Resource:   framework.Pod,
		ActionType: framework.All,
	}}
}
```

But, even when a new Pod is created, the Pod that was unscheduled by our custom plugin isn't moved to backoffQ/activeQ.

### What did you expect to happen?

when a new Pod is created, the Pod unscheduled by our custom plugin is moved to backoffQ/activeQ.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a custom plugin that has pod events in EventsToRegister.
2. create a new Pod that the custom plugin will reject.
3. create another new Pod that makes the Pod created in (1) schedulable.
4. you can see the Pod created in (1) isn't scheduled immediately (it should've been scheduled immediately after (3) because (3) should move the Pod created in (1) to activeQ/backoffQ.)

### Anything else we need to know
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduling queue's preCheck mechanism assumes a scheduler configuration with only built-in plugins and does not handle external/custom plugins properly, causing pods rejected by these custom plugins to not be moved to the active or backoff queue when new Pods are created. This incompatibility leads to pods staying unscheduled because QHint replaces preCheck's functionality but isn't designed for extensibility with custom plugins.
FIX: feat: disable preCheck when QHint is enabled
FILES: pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/scheduling_queue.go, pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go, pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers_test.go

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

TITLE: Assigned Pod add/update events don't requeue Pods without PodAffinity
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?



- AssignedPodAdded(): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b529e6ff1c7edb3bb1eaca185b9662d8e42ac2d0/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L1044
- AssignedPodUpdated(): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b529e6ff1c7edb3bb1eaca185b9662d8e42ac2d0/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L1069


When assigned Pods are created/updated, cluster events (Pod/Add or Pod/Update) should be delivered for all plugins that subscribe those events. But, actually `getUnschedulablePodsWithMatchingAffinityTerm` pre-filters Pods to receive those events based on Pods' affinity and `pod.Status.Resize`. - meaning only PodAffinity/NodeResourceFit receive them actually.

The problem here is similar to #110175 - in in-tree plugins, PodAffinity, PodTopologySpread and NodeResourceFit subscribe Pod add and/or update events. And, Pods rejected by PodTopologySpread will never be requeued to activeQ by Pod-related events. The same happens for custom plugins registering pod add and/or update events.


### What did you expect to happen?

All Pods will get chances to get back to activeQ by Pod-related events.

### How can we reproduce it (a
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the mechanism that requeued Pods on pod add/update events filtered Pods only based on PodAffinity and resizing status, ignoring Pods rejected by PodTopologySpread. This selective event delivery prevented Pods rejected by PodTopologySpread and other plugins with similar event subscriptions from being requeued after pod-related events, causing them to get stuck unrescheduled.
FIX: Fix a bug that when PodTopologySpread rejects Pods, they may be stuck in Pending state for 5 min in a worst case scenario.
The same problem could happen with custom plugins which have Pod/Add or Pod/Update in EventsToRegister,
which is also solved with this PR, but only when the feature flag SchedulerQueueingHints is enabled.

After control plane nodes recreation and after kube-apiserver being brought again. In some scenarios (we are still investigating the exact scenario), we found some request (mostly `GET openapi/v2`) may cause nil pointer panic in kube-apiserver:

And it seems to only happen when the request is routed to `kube-aggregator`, no similar issues on `kube-apiserv
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the panic was a race condition during the startup of the kube-aggregator's openapi aggregation. FIX: Fix regression with adding aggregated apiservices panicking and affected health check introduced in release v1.28.0

TITLE: Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L984-L1006
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L519-L543
4.  Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

```
Jul 25 1
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is a concurrency race in kubelet's device manager when allocating GPU devices to pods. The mutex guarding the allocated devices map is unlocked while calling out to device plugins, allowing concurrent updates and leading to inconsistent or nil map values. This causes the allocation function to panic due to nil map assignments when multiple GPU-using pods are created or deleted concurrently.
FIX: Fix kubelet panic when allocate resource for pod.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the code assumes that the YAML input offset after decoding is always greater than or equal to the consumed bytes by the underlying stream when calling d.stream.Consume. However, this assumption is not validated, and when the YAML data length is shorter than the previously read JSON data length, the subtraction (d.yaml.InputOffset() - d.stream.Consumed()) becomes negative. This causes a negative slice bound in the Consume() method, leading to a panic.

claims.text: The panic is caused by line 337 in decoder.go where 'd.stream.Consume(d.yaml.InputOffset() - d.stream.Consumed())' is called without checking if the subtraction is negative, which can happen if YAML data length is less than JSON data previously read.
The code assumes the YAML input offset is always >= the stream consumed bytes, but this is not validated, causing a negative slice bounds error and subsequent panic.

TITLE: DRA: Kubelet doesn't report anything when it fails to prepare dynamic resources
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When `PrepareResource` API fails there is no way to understand what happens because error is not reported.

Error should be either logged or, better event should be recorded, so user would see it in the `kubelet describe pod` output.

+++ b/test/e2e/dra/test-driver/deploy/example/pod-inline.yaml

```

2. Create a pod: ```kubectl apply -f test/e2e/dra/test-driver/deploy/example/pod-inline.yaml```

TITLE: DRA: kubelet: crash when plugin returns nil UnprepareResourceResponse
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

protobuf doesn't require that objects get encoded when they are empty. This can lead to a nil pointer in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124042 (although that's probably an error because some information is needed) and in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/20d0ab7ae808aaddb1556c3c38ca0607663c50ac/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/dra/v1alpha3/api.pb.go#L255 (happened in practice).

The result is a crash of kubelet:
```
E0305 14:50:50.162844   10432 runtime.go:79] Observed a panic: "invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference" (runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference)
goroutine 883 [running]:
k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime.logPanic({0x3de2d20?, 0x6fc0d90})
	/go/src/kubernetes/vendor/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime/runtime.go:75 +0x85
k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime.HandleCrash({0x0, 0x0, 0x0?})
	/go/src/kubernetes/vendor/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime/runtime.go:49 +0x6b
panic({0x3de2d20?, 0x6fc0d90?})
	/usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:914 +0x21f
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra.(*ManagerImpl).UnprepareResources(0xc00097b998, 0xc000d48900)
	/go/src/kubernetes/pkg/
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet code did not handle the case where the Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver returns a nil pointer for the NodePrepareResources or NodeUnprepareResources response. Because protobuf encoding can omit empty objects leading to nil pointers, this caused a nil pointer dereference panic in the kubelet.
FIX: kubelet no longer crashes when a DRA driver returns a nil as part of the Node(Un)PrepareResources response instead of an empty struct (did not affect drivers written in Go, first showed up with a driver written in Rust).
FILES: pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug arises because NodeUnprepareResources does not block the pod removal process when a pod has zero terminationGracePeriod, leading to premature deletion of claim info cache entries. This causes later kubelet operations to fail retrieving claim info for existing claims, resulting in a locked cache operation error. Essentially, the resource unprepare phase is skipped or completed too early due to the zero terminationGracePeriod edge case, causing race conditions in the claimInfoCache and loss of claim information.

claims.text: The error "unable to get claim info for claim external-claim in namespace default" happens in claimInfoCache.get as shown in the stack trace that includes claiminfo.go:173 and manager.go:383 indicating the problem lies in the claimInfoCache management and usage within DRA Manager.

Stress testing on a dynamically created and deleted ResourceClaim implies a race condition in managing the claim cache because the cache is losing track of the claim entries that should exist, making the kubelet unable to retrieve claim info.

Past incident kb-123474 confirmed that concurrent unsynchronized map writes in claimInfoCache led to race crashes and eventual data integrity issues, indicating the cache needs proper synchronization and order of operations to avoid inconsistencies.

Lack of a call to ManagerImpl.prepareResources in the failure trace suggests the kubelet may conclude resource preparation prematurely or not do it at all when terminationGracePeriod is zero, allowing pod removal to proceed while claim entries still exist or are expected later.

Previous incidents and code suggest the DRA Manager must carefully synchronize prepare and unprepare phases to keep claimInfoCache consistent; skipping or racing these phases leads to stale or missing cache entries causing pod failure on restart or container start.

TITLE: Code Generation Produces Ambiguous Fields and Duplicate Methods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The changes introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121439 require that all types used with the generated clients implement both `runtime.Object` and `meta.Object`. In order to comply with this, we started embedding `metav1.ObjectMeta` in our API types that were missing it. However, we noticed that, for some of our types, the generator generates code with ambiguous fields and duplicate methods.

For example, consider the following case where both `metav1.ObjectMeta` and `MyEmbeddedType`, which are embedded in `MyType`, contain a `Namespace` field:

```


type MyType struct {
	metav1.TypeMeta   `json:",inline"`
	metav1.ObjectMeta `json:"metadata,omitempty"`

	MyEmbeddedType `json:"myEmbeddedType"`
}

type MyEmbeddedType struct {
	Namespace string `json:"namespace"`
}
```

This will generate code like:

```
func (b *MyTypeApplyConfiguration) WithNamespace(value string) *MyTypeApplyConfiguration {
	b.ensureObjectMetaApplyConfigurationExists()
	b.Namespace = &value
	return b
}
```

Here, `b.Namespace` is invalid because that field is present in both embedded types.



### What did you expect to happen?

Generat
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the code generator (applyconfiguration-gen) does not handle the presence of multiple embedded structs that contain fields with the same name. This leads the generator to produce methods and field accesses that are ambiguous or duplicated because it does not qualify or differentiate these fields based on their embedding types. The defect is that applyconfiguration-gen assumes unique member names at the top level without considering embedded struct conflicts.
FIX: applyconfiguration-gen no longer generates duplicate methods and ambiguous member accesses when types end up with multiple members of the same name (through embedded structs).
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/examples/client-go/pkg/client/applyconfiguration/cr/v1/example.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/client/applyconfiguration/apiextensions/v1/customresourcedefinition.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/client/applyconfiguration/apiextensions/v1beta1/customresourcedefinition.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/mutatingwebhookconfiguration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/namedrulewithoperations.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/rulewithoperations.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/validatingadmissionpolicy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/validatingadmissionpolicybinding.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/validatingwebhookconfiguration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1alpha1/namedrulewithoperations.go

TITLE: Sometime Liveness/Readiness Probes fail because of net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
SYMPTOM: **What happened**:
In my cluster sometimes readiness the probes are failing. But the application works fine.
```
Apr 06 18:15:14 kubenode** kubelet[34236]: I0406 18:15:14.056915   34236 prober.go:111] Readiness probe for "default-nginx-daemonset-4g6b5_default(a3734646-77fd-11ea-ad94-509a4c9f2810):nginx" failed (failure): Get http://172.18.123.127:80/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
```

**What you expected to happen**:
Successful Readiness Probe.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
We have few clusters with different workloads.
Only in cluster with big number of short living pods we have this issue.
But not on all nodes.
We can't reproduce this error on other our clusters (that have same configuration but different workload).
How i found the issue?
I deployed a daemonset:
```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: default-nginx-daemonset
  namespace: default
  labels:
    k8s-app: default-nginx
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      name: default-nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: default-nginx

ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that kubelet readiness and liveness probes open many short-lived network connections that enter the TIME-WAIT state, which by default lasts 60 seconds. This causes exhaustion of network resources like ephemeral ports and conntrack entries on nodes with many pods and high probe rates, leading to probe failures.
FIX: kubelet TCP and HTTP probes are more effective using networking resources: conntrack entries, sockets, ... 
This is achieved by reducing the TIME-WAIT state of the connection to 1 second, instead of the defaults 60 seconds. This allows kubelet to free the socket, and free conntrack entry and ephemeral port associated.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/prober/scale_test.go, pkg/probe/dialer_others.go, pkg/probe/dialer_windows.go, pkg/probe/http/http.go, pkg/probe/tcp/tcp.go

TITLE: kube-apiserver using unregistered and unusual label
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The code at
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86f3fa94f1b75da275a8040e4155840a7b473dc1/pkg/controlplane/instance.go#L126 specifies a ~annotation~ label that API servers set on Leases (each API server registers its own lease).

https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/#api-server-identity is likely to document this once v1.26 is released; the alpha for API server identity didn't get documented.

Here's the problems:
- as a project, we use `kubernetes.io` as the domain for labels and annotations - see https://k8s.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/
  - there are a couple of exceptions in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/audit-annotations/, FWIW
- if we document and register this `k8s.io/component` label, people may well confuse it with https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#app-kubernetes-io-component and use the wrong thing

### What did you expect to happen?

I guess ideally we'd have proposed and then been able to review docs for this when it went alpha, and in that alternative history the discrepancy would have been much more obvious, and it could have been fixed 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the API server was using a non-standard, unregistered label `k8s.io/component` for identifying leases, which conflicted with Kubernetes label conventions and could be easily confused with an existing well-known label `app.kubernetes.io/component`. This violated Kubernetes labeling best practices and conventions causing potential confusion and improper usage.
FIX: Renamed API server identity Lease labels to use the key `apiserver.kubernetes.io/identity`

I created an ephemeral container for a Static Pod using the `kubectl debug` command. The command succeed.

### What did you expect to happen?

I

TITLE: Request timeout not respected while listing from storage
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is possible to issue a list request which exceeds the duration set by the request-timeout apiserver flag. The request-timeout flag does not appear to be enforced when the apiserver is decoding the response from etcd. 

Specifically, listing a large number of CRDs from etcd can result in high request latency from using json encoding compared to protobuf encoding. While overall etcd latency is low, the overall listing from storage latency may be over the 1 minute timeout, particularly if the apiserver needs to fetch multiple pages from etcd.


### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the list requests to be subject to the duration specified by the request-timeout flag when this latency is coming from the listing from storage phase of the request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create 4000 CRs and list all the objects from etcd in 2 pages of 2000 objects. If the time to list 1 page + decode takes around 50s, listing 2 pages will result in the listing from storage phase of the request taking  around 1 minute and 40s before the request fails and the client is returned a 500 response code.

Logs for apiserver Tr
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the apiserver's request-timeout enforcement does not cover the duration spent decoding data fetched from etcd. When a large list request is served, the total time including multiple pages fetched and JSON decoding can exceed the timeout without being interrupted, resulting in request latency longer than configured. This is because the timeout mechanism only covers the etcd fetch phase but not the decoding phase.
FIX: Add apiserver.latency.k8s.io/decode-response-object annotation to the audit log to record the decoding time
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/request/webhook_duration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go

TITLE: API emulation versioning seems break Cohabitating Resources overwriting
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have an extension apiserver, and I was trying to upgrading the dependency `k8s.io/apiserver`.  In our code, we have a serval resources has its `Cohabitating Resources`, and we expect the storage version is their `Cohabitating Resources`.

for example, we have a resource `machine` in both `raw` and `core` group, and they are wired up by `AddCohabitatingResources` method, and expected encoded as `raw` to storage.

```

However, this seems broken after upgrade to v1.31, so I did some invertgation by myself, and I find the storage version is changed by `BackwardCompatibileStorageEncodingFor`  here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/403301bfdf2c7312591077827abd2e72f445a53a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/storage/storage_factory.go#L244-L257

storage version semantic of `Cohabitation Resources` would be honored.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

th
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the newer implementation of BackwardCompatibleStorageEncodingFor did not honor the chosen storage resource specified by cohabitating resources, breaking the expected storage versioning semantics for those resources. FIX: Fixes a 1.31 regression with API emulation versioning honors cohabitating resources

TITLE: ResourceClaimParametersRef.APIGroup allows APIversion values
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Following YAML file is accepted without error. Notice the `spec.parametersRef.apiGroup` field, it is an `APIVersion` instead of `APIGroup`, containing `/` character. This can lead to an issue when resource driver generates structured parameters' in-tree `ResourceClaimParameters` object with `generatedFrom.apiGroup` being just `APIGroup` without version. The DRA scheduler plugin will try to match the parameters object based on the reference here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/be4afb9ef90b19ccb6f7e595cbdb247e088b2347/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L1066

In latest master the code appears to use an indexer, and the issue might be hidden, if applicable at all. I did not check the reproducibility in master yet. However, main question is whether the `APIGroup` should allow `APIVersion` value with `/` character in general.

```YAML
apiVersion: gpu.resource.intel.com/v1alpha2
kind: GpuClaimParameters
metadata:
  name: delayed-claim-external-gpu
spec:
  count: 1
  type: "gpu"
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: delayed-claim-external-gpu
spec:
  resourceCl
ROOT CAUSE: The ResourceClaimParametersReference API allows an invalid value in the apiGroup field where an API version string (which contains a '/') is accepted instead of a valid API group name. This incorrect acceptance is due to missing validation constraints on the apiGroup field, which allows API version values containing characters like '/'. This leads to issues when resource driver generated parameters and the scheduler plugin try to match references by apiGroup but only expect a proper group without version suffixes.
FIX: DRA: enhance validation for the ResourceClaimParametersReference and ResourceClassParametersReference with the following rules:

1. `apiGroup`: If set, it must be a valid DNS subdomain (e.g. 'example.com').
2. `kind` and `name`: It must be valid path segment name. It may not be '.' or '..' and it may not contain '/' and '%' characters.

```

This error seems to be flaky, occasionally the dry run passes for one or both of them.

### What did you expect to happen?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a new Kubernetes cluster
2. Install a CRD that has an old
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by changes introduced in Kubernetes 1.27 that refactored the conversion process for custom resources using a conversion strategy of `None`. The missing metadata caused the conversion to fail because the code incorrectly handled or omitted essential metadata fields when no conversion webhook was used.
FIX: Fixes a regression in 1.27.0 that resulted in "missing metadata in converted object" errors when modifying objects for multi-version custom resource definitions with a conversion strategy of `None`.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because when the 'limit' parameter is provided alongside a large 'resourceVersion', the list request bypasses the internal watch cache and directly queries etcd. Etcd returns an error "required revision is a future revision" for resourceVersions it does not yet have. Instead of translating this to an expected 504 timeout with a controlled error message, the API server propagates the etcd 500 error response back to the client. Without 'limit', the request uses the watch cache which handles unavailable resourceVersions with a 504 response appropriately.

claims.text: Passing a large resourceVersion with a limit causes the request to hit etcd directly, leading to etcd returning "required revision is a future revision" error and the API server responding with 500.
Removing the limit parameter causes the request to use the internal watch cache, which returns a 504 Timeout with an appropriate message when resourceVersion is too large.
The watch cache and direct etcd queries handle unavailable resourceVersions differently, with the watch cache translating them into expected 504 errors, while direct etcd queries return a 500 error.

triage.summary: In Kubernetes v1.32, applying a Job with spec.completions=0 and spec.suspend=true results in Job status showing conditions with SuccessCriteriaMet but missing terminal Complete condition, and Job status shows Running instead of Complete as in v1.31.

TITLE: A Job might finish with ready!=0, terminating!=0
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Job is declared Failed, the running Pods still count as ready.
This causes problems for higher level controllers that use the Failed/Completed conditions to do usage accounting. If the job is marked as finished before all the pods finish, the accounting is inaccurate.

### What did you expect to happen?

A few options (non-necessarily exclusive), in order of my preference:
1. The job not to be declared Completed/Failed until all the Pods have finished. This is possibly a breaking change. As a mitigation, we can use the `FailureTarget` or `SuccessCriteriaMet` conditions to provide early feedback to controllers that a Job is marked for failure.
2. ~Do not count Pods with a deletionTimestamp as ready. (Possibly a breaking change)~
3. ~We just consider ready=0 if setting a finished condition~
4. Continue syncing a Job even after the Failed condition is added, until ready/terminating fields are zero.

Options 2 and 3 don't satisfy the requirement of proper accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Use this Job (note backoffLimit: 0):
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: inde
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the Job was marked as Failed or Completed as soon as failure or success conditions were met, without waiting for all Pods to reach a terminal state. This caused running Pods to still be counted as ready, leading to inaccurate accounting in higher-level controllers that rely on Job conditions.
FIX: Delay setting terminal Job conditions until all pods are terminal.

Additionally, the FailureTarget condition is also added to the Job object in the first Job
status update as soon as the failure conditions are met (backoffLimit is exceeded, maxFailedIndexes, 
or activeDeadlineSeconds is exceeded).

Similarly, the SuccessCriteriaMet condition is added in the first update as soon as the expected number
of pod completions is reached.

Also, introduce the following validation rules for Job status when JobManagedBy is enabled:
1. the count of ready pods is less or equal than active
2. when transitioning to terminal phase for Job, the number of terminating pods is 0
3. terminal Job conditions (Failed and Complete) should be preceded by adding the corresponding interim conditions: FailureTarget and SuccessCriteriaMet
FILES: pkg/apis/batch/validation/validation.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, pkg/controller/job/success_policy.go, pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy.go, pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy_test.go, test/e2e/apps/job.go, test/e2e/framework/job/wait.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: Job controller reports the count of ready pods with unnecessary delay
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When Job controller is deleting pods the counter in the status.ready field does not reflect this properly (there is a delay until the cache is refreshed). This affects the scenarios of terminating job, suspended job, and excess pods deleted.

### What did you expect to happen?

The ready field is updated as soon as the delete requests are sent successfully, in sync with the status.active field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. To see this you can scale down a job, use the following yaml:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: simple-job
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: 'worker'
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import time
          time.sleep(300)
```

2. Watch for the job updates with the following watcher:
```
kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,READY:.object.status.ready,ACTIVE:.object.status.active,TERMINATING:.object.status.terminat
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Job controller counts ready pods only among the currently active pods during deletion, but since the number of active pods updates asynchronously and may decrease after the count was made, the ready pod count does not get updated promptly to reflect pods that are terminating or deleted. This lag causes stale ready counts until the cache refreshes.
FIX: Now the .status.ready field is tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: Job terminates when FailureTarget=False condition is added manually
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When the FailureTarget=False condition is added manually, then the Job terminates.

### What did you expect to happen?

The condition should be ignored by the Job controller.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Prepare the `job.yaml` like this:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: test-job
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: test-container
        image: busybox
        command: ["sleep", "3m"]
      restartPolicy: Never
```
2. Run the following script to repro:
```sh
kubectl create -f job.yaml

NAMESPACE=${NAMESPACE:-default}
JOB_NAME=${JOB_NAME:-test-job}

kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.ready}'=1 job $JOB_NAME -n $NAMESPACE

JOB_JSON=$(kubectl get job $JOB_NAME -n $NAMESPACE -o json)

UPDATED_JOB_JSON=$(echo $JOB_JSON | jq --arg type "FailureTarget" \
                                         --arg status "False" \
                                         --arg reason "ManualUpdateByScript" \
'.status.conditions += [{"type": $type, "status": $status, "reason": $reason, "lastTransitionTime": (now | strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"))}]')

ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller does not discriminate between FailureTarget conditions based on their Status value; any FailureTarget condition, even with Status=False, triggers Job termination logic. This means that manually adding a FailureTarget=False condition incorrectly causes the Job to be marked as failed and terminated.
FIX: job_controller: Ignore FailureTarget JobCondition with Status != True
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an intern
ROOT CAUSE: The job controller initiates creation of replacement pods immediately upon noticing a pod deletion without waiting for the original pod to fully terminate. This premature creation can lead to multiple pods running concurrently when parallelism is set to 1, violating users' expectations and causing application failures. The controller did not implement a mechanism to delay pod creation until the pod state was confirmed as terminated.
FIX: Add implementation for PodRecreationPolicy to wait for creation of pods once the existing ones are fully terminated.
FILES: pkg/controller/controller_utils.go, pkg/controller/controller_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: Job controller reports the count of terminating pods with unnecessary delay
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When Job controller is terminating and deletes all pods the counter in the `status.terminating` field does not reflect this properly. 

### What did you expect to happen?

The counter for the terminating pods is updated as soon as Job controller has this information. Similarly as for the counter of active pods.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

0. watch the job & pod updates with the commands:
`kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,STATUS:.object.status | ts "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%.S"`
`kubectl get pods -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,PHASE:.object.status.phase,FINALIZERS:.object.metadata.finalizers,DELETION:object.metadata.deletionTimestamp,CONTAINERS:.object.status.containerStatuses | ts "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%.S"`
1. Run the Job:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: indexed-job
  labels:
    jobgroup: indexedjob
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  backoffLimit: 0
  completionMode: Indexed
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
    
ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller failed to increment the counter for terminating pods when it actively deletes pods during job termination, particularly for failed jobs. This caused the .status.terminating field to not reflect terminating pods accurately, leading to delayed or incorrect status updates.
FIX: .status.terminating field now gets tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The Kubernetes Job controller, since version 1.31, introduced interim conditions (SuccessCriteriaMet and FailureTarget) to represent early Job success or failure states before pods fully terminate, delaying the setting of terminal conditions (Complete or Failed) until all pods have finished and their finalizers are removed. For a Job with spec.completions=0 and spec.suspend=true, jobs show SuccessCriteriaMet condition but remain in "Running" status without the Complete condition until no pods are active or terminating. This delay mechanism ensures accurate resource accounting and prevents premature termination signaling when pods are still cleaning up. The 1.31 to 1.32 behavior change reflects this intentional logic to avoid marking Jobs as Complete prematurely while pods are terminating, as implemented in job_controller.go.

claims.text: The job_controller.go code manages Job status transitions by immediately appending SuccessCriteriaMet condition but delaying terminal Complete condition until all pods have been fully terminated and finalizers removed, explaining why Jobs with suspends and terminating pods show SuccessCriteriaMet but not Complete until pod finalization.

The 1.31 release introduced delaying the terminal Job conditions setting until all pods are terminal, and adding interim conditions like SuccessCriteriaMet early to indicate the Job fate without final terminal conditions, to improve accuracy for resource/quota management and usage accounting.

triage.summary: In Kubernetes 1.33, paginated LIST calls with rv="" and LIMIT set fall back unnecessarily to etcd instead of being served from cache, causing performance degradation. The root cause is that the watch_cache returns errors when snapshot is nil due to demanding an exact resource version rather than allowing NotOlderThan, leading to fallback to etcd.

TITLE: Request timeout not respected while listing from storage
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is possible to issue a list request which exceeds the duration set by the request-timeout apiserver flag. The request-timeout flag does not appear to be enforced when the apiserver is decoding the response from etcd. 

Specifically, listing a large number of CRDs from etcd can result in high request latency from using json encoding compared to protobuf encoding. While overall etcd latency is low, the overall listing from storage latency may be over the 1 minute timeout, particularly if the apiserver needs to fetch multiple pages from etcd.


### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the list requests to be subject to the duration specified by the request-timeout flag when this latency is coming from the listing from storage phase of the request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create 4000 CRs and list all the objects from etcd in 2 pages of 2000 objects. If the time to list 1 page + decode takes around 50s, listing 2 pages will result in the listing from storage phase of the request taking  around 1 minute and 40s before the request fails and the client is returned a 500 response code.

Logs for apiserver Tr
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the apiserver's request-timeout enforcement does not cover the duration spent decoding data fetched from etcd. When a large list request is served, the total time including multiple pages fetched and JSON decoding can exceed the timeout without being interrupted, resulting in request latency longer than configured. This is because the timeout mechanism only covers the etcd fetch phase but not the decoding phase.
FIX: Add apiserver.latency.k8s.io/decode-response-object annotation to the audit log to record the decoding time
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/request/webhook_duration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go

In 1.30, WATCH request is logged immediately when a watch is opened, with very low latency. There appears to be no trace of when the watch ends. This significantly impacts debugging capability for issues with establishing watches. 

Example for consecutive watches on pods opened by kube-scheduler - each appears to be lasting 8-9 minutes, everything works in the cluster, but the latency doesn't match watch length, the request is logged immediately, and with `resp=0`:
