diagnosis.root_cause: In Kubernetes 1.33, the cached paginated LIST requests with resourceVersion="" and limit set unnecessarily fall back to etcd due to an incorrect handling of cache listing errors. Specifically, when listItems calls into watchCache.listExactRV and finds the snapshot is nil (since snapshots are not enabled), it returns errors.NewResourceExpired, which the delegator interprets as cache inconsistency and causes fallback to etcd. This occurs despite the cache actually being able to serve data at least as fresh as the requested RV, because the code mistakenly expects an exact match for the RV when a NotOlderThan response would suffice.

claims.text: The CacheDelegator GETLIST function flow shows that when the cache GetList returns errors.NewResourceExpired, the request falls back to etcd GetList, indicating fallback is triggered by this error from cache listing.

In the 1.33 watch_cache.go code, the listExactRV method returns errors.NewResourceExpired if the snapshot is nil, which happens when snapshots are not enabled. This causes listItems to return error from cache listing even though the cache could serve data.

The regression from 1.32 to 1.33 was caused by a code path change that replaced the previous list not exact RV function (which provided NotOlderThan freshness) with listExactRV which demands exact RV match, causing unnecessary errors and fallback on paginated requests with limit set.

triage.summary: The systemd watchdog for kubelet starts too late, leading to it killing the kubelet if registration is slow due to lack of timely notifications. The watchdog should start as early as possible to avoid depending on kubelet initialization speed.

evidence.text:
TITLE: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and p
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cacher's readiness blocking mechanism was implemented using a sync.Cond variable that did not support context cancellation or timeouts. As a result, watch requests waiting for the cacher to become ready could be blocked indefinitely if the cacher was never marked ready, leading to infinite wait and resource exhaustion in concurrency queues.
FIX: cacher allow context cancellation if not ready
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cache_watcher_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher_whitebox_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/ready.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/ready_test.go

TITLE: kubelet GetBootTime() could drift backward for 1s
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

There are a few places in kubelet that calls `pkg/kubelet/util`.`GetBootTime()`. One such place is the kubelet `/stats/summary` endpoint where it's getting the node startTime: [ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.30.0/pkg/kubelet/server/stats/summary.go#L56)

And there's an issue in the [Linux implementation of `GetBootTime`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.31.0/pkg/kubelet/util/boottime_util_linux.go#L30) that the result is not consistent: sometimes it could drift backwards for 1s. This caused problem in certain monitoring systems where the time series database expect timestamps to be monotonically increasing.****

### What did you expect to happen?

`GetBootTime()` to return consistent result everytime it runs, more specifically the kubelet `/stats/summary` endpoint returns a consistent node startTime when kubelet restarts.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

do the following steps multiple times:

- restart kubelet
- do a http get on kubelet /stats/summary endpoint
- observe the `node`.`startTime` field in the response

you will see the node startTime could shift backwards for 1s i
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because GetBootTime() uses the current time with sub-second precision and subtracts the system uptime (which is an integer in seconds), and then truncates the result to the earlier second. When the uptime increments between calling time.Now() and unix.Sysinfo(), this subtraction can produce a result that appears to drift backward by one second.
FIX: fix node start time inconsistency in kubelet
FILES: pkg/kubelet/util/boottime_util_linux.go, pkg/kubelet/util/boottime_util_linux_test.go

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…
FILES: pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

TITLE: cronjob controller: reconsider log verbosity
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running Kubernetes 1.25.5 and trying to configure kube-controller-manager to be less verbose when logging.
We run kube-controller-manager as a static pod created by Kubelet and use the following command where we pass `--v=0`:
```
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-controller-manager
    - --feature-gates=EphemeralContainers=true,TopologyAwareHints=true
    - --allocate-node-cidrs=true
    - --authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --authorization-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --cluster-cidr=10.6.0.0/16
    - --configure-cloud-routes=false
    - --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/config/controller-manager.conf
    - --leader-elect=true
    - --node-monitor-grace-period=120s
    - --root-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/ca.pem
    - --service-account-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/ssl/signing-key.pem
    - --use-service-account-credentials
    - --v=0
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.25.5
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    livenessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        host: 127.0.0.1
        path: /healthz
        po
ROOT CAUSE: The cronjob controller uses a global logging verbosity level of 3 for its event broadcaster, which is independent of the global -v flag passed to kube-controller-manager. As a result, event messages logged with verbosity 4 are always emitted if the global level is 3, ignoring the --v flag. This causes noisy logs even when low verbosity (e.g., --v=0) is requested. The root cause is the broadcaster's logging level is hardcoded and does not depend on the passed verbosity flag.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: increase the global level for broadcaster's logging to 3 so that users can ignore event messages by lowering the logging level. It reduces information noise.

TITLE: `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` check blocks apiserver readiness for 1 minute if discovery cannot be completed
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I’m seeing some odd behavior with 1.28.2 that was not present in earlier releases, with regards to aggregated api services. It appears that the `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` is now blocking the apiserver from becoming ready for 1 minute, if discovery for an aggregated apiservice is not available when the apiserver is started. Note that this only happens if the apiservice is marked available when the apiserver is started; if it is unavailable at startup (Available status: false), or the service has no endpoints, the health check does not block and readyz returns `ok` without delay.

I am seeing this behavior in 1.28.1 and 1.28.2, but not v1.27.6 or v1.27.5

### What did you expect to happen?

apiserver becomes ready without any additional delays

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy metrics-server to a Kubernetes cluster
2. Wait for api registration for `v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io` to complete (Available status is `true`).
3. Kill the kubelet and pods on the node hosting the metrics-server pod, such that the metrics-server service continues to show available endpoints, but the endpoint is 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by the AddUpdateAPIService function simultaneously adding and updating the APIService spec during startup, rather than deferring the spec update to be handled asynchronously by the controller. This synchronous update caused race conditions and health check blocking when discovery failed, leading to readiness delays.
FIX: Fix regression with adding aggregated apiservices panicking and affected health check introduced in release v1.28.0

diagnosis.root_cause: The systemd watchdog in the kubelet only starts sending notifications after the kubelet finishes some initializations and features enabled, such as EventedPLEG. Because the watchdog goroutine with periodic notifications is launched late, any slowness in kubelet initialization delays the first notification, causing systemd to kill kubelet erroneously for missed watchdog pings.

claims.text: The systemd watchdog starts executing its periodic notification loop only when the healthChecker's Start() function is called, which happens after kubelet initializations and feature gates are enabled, as shown by healthChecker.Start(ctx) being called conditionally based on the SystemdWatchdog feature gate in pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go

In the watchdog_linux.go code, the goroutine that repeatedly calls SdNotify with the systemd watchdog is triggered inside the healthChecker's Start(), which happens after kubelet initialization, thus the first notification is not sent immediately upon process start but delayed according to initialization duration, leading to potential systemd watchdog timeout if initialization is slow

TITLE: Improve message `prefer a domain-qualified finalizer name to avoid accidental conflicts with other finalizer writers`
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

k8s component developers are using FQDNs as finalizers (e.g. `cluster.cluster.x-k8s.io` or `finalizer.acme.cert-manager.io` which triggers an error message that isn't particularly easy for an end user to understand:

`prefer a domain-qualified finalizer name to avoid accidental conflicts with other finalizer writers`

To a naive end user, a fully qualified domain name is a pretty safe thing that is unlikely to conflict with anything else  (as long as it's only used by someone from within the domain that owns it, which is a reasonable assumption).

### What did you expect to happen?

If the finalizer has `.`s inside it but no `/`, the message should suggest that finalizers need a `/`.

Something like:
`prefer a domain-qualified finalizer name including a path (/) to avoid accidental conflicts with other finalizer writers`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Do whatever it is that triggered the warning in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api/issues/10914 (this is probably simpler than installing cert-manager and asking for a certificate)

### Anything else we need to know?

#119508 introduced: https://github.com
ROOT CAUSE: The message warning about finalizer names was insufficiently precise. It did not indicate that a domain-qualified finalizer name must include a '/' path element, causing confusion since names with '.' but without '/' were accepted but still triggered a warning. This lack of clarity led users to misunderstand the format requirements for finalizer names.
FIX: Improve message prefer a domain-qualified finalizer

TITLE: [Bug] Missing constraint and validation for label selector's values
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Hello,
There are some [constraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#syntax-and-character-set) that label selector's `values` need to conform:
>* must be 63 characters or less (can be empty),
>* unless empty, must begin and end with an alphanumeric character ([a-z0-9A-Z]),
>* could contain dashes (-), underscores (_), dots (.), and alphanumerics between.

Every label selctor's `values` will be checked [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e5ba5cd2b0d3bddd4a0393b98fde14960f31a33c/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation/validation.go#L166C1-L175C2), and when values is not conforming these constraints, an error will be returned.

`nodeAfffinty.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.nodeSelectorTerms.matchExpressions.values` also needs to conform these constraints (because `matchExpressions` will be parsed as a label selector), but cccording to the [concept documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#operators) and the [API documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.31/#nodeselectorrequirement-v1-core), 
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying cause is that the system did not validate the values in NodeSelectorRequirement against label value constraints during pod creation. This lack of validation allowed invalid strings to be accepted, leading to parse errors during scheduling and causing the scheduler to reject the node selector terms silently without warning the user.
FIX: kubenetes starts validating NodeSelectorRequirement's values when creating pods.

TITLE: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an intern
ROOT CAUSE: The job controller initiates creation of replacement pods immediately upon noticing a pod deletion without waiting for the original pod to fully terminate. This premature creation can lead to multiple pods running concurrently when parallelism is set to 1, violating users' expectations and causing application failures. The controller did not implement a mechanism to delay pod creation until the pod state was confirmed as terminated.
FIX: Add implementation for PodRecreationPolicy to wait for creation of pods once the existing ones are fully terminated.
FILES: pkg/controller/controller_utils.go, pkg/controller/controller_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/indexed_job_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: Kubernetes Jobs API rapid-fire scheduling doesnt honor exponential backoff characteristics
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

# Problem

The job controller appears to "rapidly reschedule" several pods at the same time (without backing off) which ultimately appears almost like a batch or gang scheduling workflow.  

... This is the opposite of what the job docs say, bc they clearly state :
```
 The back-off limit is set by default to 6. Failed Pods associated with the Job are recreated by the Job controller with an exponential back-off delay (10s, 20s, 40s ...) capped at six minutes.
```
So, rather then, 

- 10, 20, 40, 80 wait times between trying things we are seeing
- 0, 3, 3, 3, 3 second wait times before pods are being retried

This is in the 1.25 release, but not sure if it also happens earlier.  You can see this in the latest kind version. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Jobs wouldnt schedule the same pod at rapid fire intervals

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

# Details 

Thanks to Ryan for this reproducer: 
```
apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

  name: backoff-exp

spec:

  backoffLimit: 100

  template:

    spec:

      containers:

        - name: die

          image: ubuntu


ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller's back-off logic was coupled with the workqueue's back-off mechanism, causing rapid rescheduling of failed pods without proper exponential delay. This coupling meant multiple pod failures within a reconciliation cycle did not properly aggregate back-off delays, resulting in retries being scheduled too frequently and ignoring exponential backoff requirements.
FIX: The job controller back-off logic is now decoupled from workqueue. In case of parallelism > 1, if there are multiple new failures in a reconciliation cycle, all the failures are taken into account to compute the back-off. Previously, the back-off kicked in for all types of failures; with this change, only pod failures are taken into account. If the back-off limits exceeds, the job is marked as failed immediately; before this change, the job is marked as failed in the next back-off.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

TITLE: Job controller reports the count of ready pods with unnecessary delay
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When Job controller is deleting pods the counter in the status.ready field does not reflect this properly (there is a delay until the cache is refreshed). This affects the scenarios of terminating job, suspended job, and excess pods deleted.

### What did you expect to happen?

The ready field is updated as soon as the delete requests are sent successfully, in sync with the status.active field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. To see this you can scale down a job, use the following yaml:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: simple-job
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: 'worker'
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import time
          time.sleep(300)
```

2. Watch for the job updates with the following watcher:
```
kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,READY:.object.status.ready,ACTIVE:.object.status.active,TERMINATING:.object.status.terminat
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Job controller counts ready pods only among the currently active pods during deletion, but since the number of active pods updates asynchronously and may decrease after the count was made, the ready pod count does not get updated promptly to reflect pods that are terminating or deleted. This lag causes stale ready counts until the cache refreshes.
FIX: Now the .status.ready field is tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: Job: Pod backoff calculation should not depend on failure policy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Pod backoff calculation excludes pods that match an `Ignore` rule in the failure policy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847f1758748ac357e79094c5e85029a10428e65f/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1365

This could lead to fast retries, overwhelming the control plane, if most failures match an `Ignore` rule. The semantics of `Ignore` is not to count towards the limit, but the backoff should still be respected.


### What did you expect to happen?

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job with failure policy that matches every kind of failure.
1. Use a container that always fails

You would observe immediate recreation.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

ROOT CAUSE: The backoff delay calculation for recreating pods in a Job controller excluded pods whose failures matched an 'Ignore' rule in the Job's failure policy. While 'Ignore' causes failures not to count towards the limit of retries, the backoff delay should still be applied. Excluding these pods led to the controller immediately recreating pods without respecting backoff delays, causing fast retries and overwhelming the control plane.

TITLE: The event handlers of job controller are slow
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The event handlers in job controller are much slower than other controllers. It can cause the ring buffer in the processorListener to grow unbounded when the job churn is high enough.
The processing logic in the job controller events handler appears to be more complicated than other controllers. e.g. in [updateJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L464-L504), it invokes function `cleanupPodFinalizers` that lists the pods matching some selectors and the enqueue them to another queue. Similarly in [deleteJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L508-L524).

I added some instrumenting code to understand the latency of each event handler.
For job controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.080 ms
job update event handler: 3.075 ms
job delete event handler: 3.076 ms
pod add event handler: 0.136 ms
pod update event handler: 0.709 ms
pod delete event handler: 0.405 ms

For ttl-after-completion controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.0065 ms
job update event handler: 0.024 ms

T
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the slowness is that the job controller's event handlers perform complex and expensive operations directly within the event handler methods, such as listing pods and enqueuing them, instead of deferring such processing to the controller's main reconcile loop. This design leads to high latency and potential buildup of events, especially under high job churn.
FIX: Improve performance of the job controller when handling job update events.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the Job controller's pod backoff store uses a key based solely on the Job's namespace and name, without incorporating the Job's unique UID. When a Job and its Pods are deleted and a new Job with the same namespace/name is created before backoff records from the old Job are cleaned, the controller mistakenly applies the old Job's backoff delays to the new Job. This causes unexpected Pod creation delays for newly created Jobs with reused names.

claims.text: The podBackoffStore in job_controller.go uses a string key composed of Job namespace and name, without UID, to track backoff records, leading to reuse of old backoff records for new Jobs with the same keys.
The ticket's detailed timeline shows that backoff records from a deleted Job remain keyed by namespace/name, which causes the new Job with the same name to be subject to backoff delays incorrectly.
A suggested fix is to key backoff records by Job UID rather than namespace/name to prevent old backoff records affecting new Jobs.

TITLE:  kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:
```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-LOAD-BALANCER dst,dst -j RETURN

TITLE: Document and test minimum privileges needed to run kube-proxy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running containers in privileged mode is not recommended as privileged containers run with all [linux capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html) enabled and can access the host's resources. Running containers in privileged mode opens number of security threads such as breakout to underlying host OS.

Currently the kube-proxy DaemonSet runs in privileged mode.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/863a462eeccca4c24bf4c4e9012f5ebccade70a2/cluster/addons/kube-proxy/kube-proxy-ds.yaml#L50-L51

https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy describes how to run kube-proxy in "rootless". To my understanding "rootless" != non-privileged mode but this configuration can be also used for running in non-privileged mode. However I see that following issues with it:
1. In the provided kube-proxy component config in https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy we have to disable certain settins to prevent kube-proxy from ensuring sysctls (which is allowed only in privileged container).

But when I tried to run kube-proxy with the prov
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because kube-proxy requires setting certain sysctls that need privileged container mode, but there was no mechanism to run these privileged operations separately from the main non-privileged kube-proxy process. This forced kube-proxy to run fully privileged or fail when run with lowered privileges, with no way to disable these sysctl settings via configuration.
FIX: Added a new `--init-only` command line flag to `kube-proxy`. Setting the flag makes `kube-proxy` perform its initial configuration that requires privileged mode, and then exit. The `--init-only` mode is intended to be executed in a privileged init container, so that the main container may run with a stricter `securityContext`.

TITLE: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersRe
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. Since the change trackers use their own mutexes independent from the proxier's, a new event could be processed between these calls, leading to inconsistent state and some endpoint updates being missed.
FIX: Fixes a race condition in the iptables mode of kube-proxy in 1.27 and later
that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a
new endpoint, the rules for the new endpoint might not be added until
much later).
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/endpointslicecache.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/service.go, pkg/proxy/service_test.go

TITLE: HPA with container metrics fails when any pod is not in a ready state
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We've noticed that our HPA will stay at it's current scale and not make decisions when a pod is in an un-Ready state. IE a single pod is in CrashLoopBackoff and the HPA shows:

```
...
resource cpu of container "mycontainer" on pods  (as a percentage of request):     <unknown> / 50%
...
Warning  FailedGetResourceMetric  78s (x7 over 4m7s)  horizontal-pod-autoscaler  unable to get metric cpu: failed to get container metrics: container guides3 not present in metrics for pod namesapce/mycontainer-20240904t1338-433ca6a1-db998df74-s5rfh
```

That particular pod was in CrashLoopBackoff at the time and it wasn't until i removed it was it able to make scaling decisions

We're also running istio so there is another container in these pods and it's running ok; this may be why it's showing up in the metrics but unable to get info on the main container

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the HPA to ignore pods in this state and use only the Ready pods for its decisions

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Setup an HPA with container based metrics
Put one of the pods in bad state, could just have a single pod con
ROOT CAUSE: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) code prematurely fails and stops making scaling decisions if any pod's container metrics are missing, which can occur when a pod is not in a Ready state or a container is crashed or terminated. Instead of ignoring such pods, the HPA errors out, preventing scaling calculations from proceeding with the available valid pod metrics.
FIX: HPA's with ContainerResource metrics will no longer error when container metrics are missing, instead they will use the same logic Resource metrics are using to make calculations

TITLE: HPA metric got stuck at a random value and not scaling down after reaching max replica count
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I utilize two customized metrics, A and B, in my HPA system. A is a gauge-based metric called SLA Metric, while B is a count-based metric that tracks failed requests with HTTP status code 502 or 503 from Istio. These metrics are scraped by Prometheus.

To use custom metrics in HPA, we're employing Kube Metrics Adapter [link](https://github.com/zalando-incubator/kube-metrics-adapter). When the application load increases, the value of the SLA Metric also increases, and then the pods scale up until they reach the maximum replica count as expected.
However, the problem arises when the load dissipates, and the pods never scale down. Despite the SLA Metric's value being below the target in Prometheus, the HPA description still displays the metric value with a stale value that can be above or below the target.

One possible reason for this is that Metric B, which relies on Istio requests, shows up as unknown since there have been no failed requests with the 502 or 503 status codes. Thus, the Prometheus query fails.
We have noticed this behavior after upgrading Kube from version 1.21 to 1.24 and changing the HPA version from autoscaling/v2beta2 to autoscaling/v2
ROOT CAUSE: The HPA controller had an edge case where if a custom metric became unavailable (returned as unknown), the controller would not update the status metrics while updating the replica count. This caused the HPA to retain stale metric values and prevented scaling down even when the actual metric values fell below the target.
FIX: hpa: always update status metrics when updating the replica count
FILES: pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Resizing pod gets stuck if limit is not configured
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Resizing CPU requests gets stuck in `InProgress` if the CPU limit is not configured:
```
$ kubectl patch pod resize-pod --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"resize-container", "resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"300m"}}}]}}'
pod/resize-pod patched
$ sleep 300
$ kubectl get pod resize-pod -o jsonpath='spec: {.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\nallocatedResources: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].allocatedResources}{"\nstatus: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].resources}{"\nresize: "}{.status.resize}{"\n"}'
spec: {"requests":{"cpu":"300m","memory":"200Mi"}}
allocatedResources: {"cpu":"300m","memory":"200Mi"}
status: {"requests":{"cpu":"200m","memory":"200Mi"}}
resize: InProgress
```

The internal behavior in kubelet varies depending on other resource limits configuration.
- If the limit for another resource is also not configured, no action is computed at `computePodResizeAction()`:
  ```
  Jul 26 13:43:09 kind-control-plane kubelet[708]: I0726 13:43:09.494698     708 kuberuntime_manager.go:1051] "computePodActions got for pod" podActions="KillPod: false, CreateSandbox: false, UpdatePodResources: false, Attempt: 0, InitContainersToStart: [], Containers
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the pod resizing logic in kubelet did not account for containers without resource limits set. Specifically, the code assumed CPU limits were always present, causing failure or no action when limits were missing. This led to resize operations getting stuck in an 'InProgress' state because the code failed to compute or apply resize actions properly without limits information.
FIX: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Enable resizing containers without limits

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Backoff problem when quickly reverting resize patch
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

While working on #125202 , issue with backoff was discovered resulting to slow reconcile when quickly reverting resize patch. This can be reproduced please check https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125205#issuecomment-2203184854 ,  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125205#issuecomment-2143527472.

Backoff issue does not happen on v1.30 or older please check https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125205#issuecomment-2203224319

### What did you expect to happen?

After patching forwards and patching backwards a pod which has a container whose `resizePolicy` is `RestartContainer`and a container whose `restartPolicy`is `RestartContainer` , pod should reach its initial state without any backoff delay introduced.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

<details>

```console
for l in `seq 301 310`; do kubectl patch pod resize-pod --patch "{\"spec\":{\"containers\":[{\"name\":\"c2\", \"resources\":{\"limits\":{\"memory\":\"${l}Mi\"}}}]}}"; sleep 3; done

$ kubectl get pod resize-pod -w
NAME         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
resize-pod   3/3     Running   0          14s
resize-pod   3/3 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused because the backoff delay for container restarts was not reset when the pod's resource resize patch was quickly reverted. This led to a slow reconcile process due to the backoff mechanism still being in effect, even though the container state returned to the initial state.
FIX: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Fix backoff problem when quickly reverting resize patch

diagnosis.root_cause: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) controller reports FailedRescale errors immediately upon encountering an update conflict during the scale subresource update to the target Deployment without retrying internally. This happens because the update call to the scale subresource returns an error when the Deployment's resourceVersion is modified concurrently, and the HPA controller does not perform retries before emitting the error event, causing noisy and unnecessary FailedRescale errors under legitimate concurrent updates.

claims.text: The code in pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go (code-1) shows that when the HPA controller attempts to update the scale subresource of the target deployment and it fails due to conflict errors, it immediately records a FailedRescale event and returns without any retry logic.

The error typically arises due to concurrent updates to the deployment's resourceVersion by other controllers or CI/CD processes causing update conflicts during scaling attempts, indicating a race condition between the HPA controller and other actors modifying the deployment concurrently.

Since the HPA controller lacks internal retry logic on update conflicts in the scaling operation, transient conflicts produce FailedRescale errors that are noisy but do not affect actual scaling success on retries.

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

[Process stats](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/stats/v1alpha1#ProcessStats) are not currently returned in kubelet summary API.



### What did you expect to happen?

[Process stats](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/stats/v1alpha1#ProcessStats) are returned correctly in kubelet summary API.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start a cluster (using kind cluster from master)

```
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                 STATUS   ROLES           AGE     VERSION
kind-control-plane   Ready    control-plane   7m49s   v1.27.0-alpha.0.1120+56a14025b06734
kind-worker          Ready    <none>          7m27s   v1.27.0-alpha.0.1120+56a14025b06734
```

3. Launch a pod and consume a few pids, e.g. 10 pids

$ kubectl run -i --tty --rm debug --image=k8s.gcr.io/busybox:latest --restart=Never -- /bin/sh
/ # for i in $(seq 1 10); do sleep 99999999 & done

PID   USER     COMMAND
    1 root     /bin/sh
   16 root     sleep 99999999
   17 root     sleep 99999999

ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Kubelet's eviction logic and stats providers did not properly calculate or report process counts (PIDs) for pods. This caused the process stats to always show zero in the summary API, which is why process-based eviction never triggered. The underlying defect was incomplete or incorrect integration of process counting from cAdvisor and CRI stats providers into the Kubelet's eviction subsystem and Metrics API.
FIX: Fix a bug where the Kubelet didn't calculate the process usage of pods correctly, leading to pods never getting evicted for PID use.

TITLE: [Bug] Missing constraint and validation for label selector's values
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Hello,
There are some [constraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#syntax-and-character-set) that label selector's `values` need to conform:
>* must be 63 characters or less (can be empty),
>* unless empty, must begin and end with an alphanumeric character ([a-z0-9A-Z]),
>* could contain dashes (-), underscores (_), dots (.), and alphanumerics between.

Every label selctor's `values` will be checked [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e5ba5cd2b0d3bddd4a0393b98fde14960f31a33c/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation/validation.go#L166C1-L175C2), and when values is not conforming these constraints, an error will be returned.

`nodeAfffinty.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.nodeSelectorTerms.matchExpressions.values` also needs to conform these constraints (because `matchExpressions` will be parsed as a label selector), but cccording to the [concept documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#operators) and the [API documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.31/#nodeselectorrequirement-v1-core), 
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying cause is that the system did not validate the values in NodeSelectorRequirement against label value constraints during pod creation. This lack of validation allowed invalid strings to be accepted, leading to parse errors during scheduling and causing the scheduler to reject the node selector terms silently without warning the user.
FIX: kubenetes starts validating NodeSelectorRequirement's values when creating pods.
FILES: pkg/api/node/util.go, pkg/api/persistentvolume/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util_test.go, pkg/api/pod/warnings.go, pkg/api/pod/warnings_test.go, pkg/apis/core/helper/helpers.go, pkg/apis/core/helper/helpers_test.go, pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go, pkg/apis/core/validation/validation_test.go

TITLE: Server-side apply has trouble with empty map
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Every time I server-side apply a `Deployment` with `spec.template.metadata.annotations: {}`, the `resourceVersion` updates. Nothing about my manifest changes between applies; if I map `annotations` to the empty map, `kubectl apply --server-side` the same manifest updates the `resourceVersion`. With client-side apply, the `resourceVersion` stays the same as long as my manifest remains constant, even if `annotations: {}`.

I read in #70281 that Kubernetes should treat absent keys, empty values (in this case, an empty map), and `null` values the same. I observe that leaving the `annotations` key out and `annotations: null` behave as expected, not modifying the `Deployment` and leaving `resourceVersion` the same, but empty map `{}` behaves as described above.

If we cannot change this behavior, I'd at least like to understand the rationale behind it.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected my `Deployment` object to stay the same between identical server-side applies, where the manifest file content was exactly the same, regardless of the value of `spec.template.metadata.annotations`. A different `resourceVersion` every apply indicates that the obje
ROOT CAUSE: The server-side apply mechanism treats empty maps (`{}`) as different from nil or absent maps in the live object, causing repeated modifications with no semantic change. This happens because empty maps are not normalized to nil before comparison, leading the apply process to think there is a change and updating the resourceVersion.
FIX: Fix bug where Server Side Apply causing spurious resourceVersion bumps on no-op patches containing empty maps.

As a result, StatefulSet API objects bypass this critical validation step, allowing invalid or missing 'whenUnsatisfiable' values to pass and causing pod creation failures at runtime.

claims.text: The function validateTopologySpreadConstraints in pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go performs validation of topologySpreadConstraints, including presence and correctness checks for whenUnsatisfiable, but this validation is invoked only on PodSpecs.

Since the validation of StatefulSet spec templates does not call or reuse this PodSpec validation function, StatefulSets can accept invalid or missing whenUnsatisfiable fields, unlike Deployments whose validation rejects such invalid specs.

TITLE: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the ClusterRole for service-account-issuer-discovery defines permissions for nonResourceURLs without trailing slashes, but the OpenAPI spec (swagger.json) documents these URLs with trailing slashes. This mismatch causes RBAC authorization to fail for legally formed requests that append a trailing slash, since the policy does not allow those exact paths.
FIX: Add slash ended urls for service-account-issuer-discovery to match API in swagger
FILES: plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/testdata/cluster-roles.yaml

TITLE: `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` check blocks apiserver readiness for 1 minute if discovery cannot be completed
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I’m seeing some odd behavior with 1.28.2 that was not present in earlier releases, with regards to aggregated api services. It appears that the `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` is now blocking the apiserver from becoming ready for 1 minute, if discovery for an aggregated apiservice is not available when the apiserver is started. Note that this only happens if the apiservice is marked available when the apiserver is started; if it is unavailable at startup (Available status: false), or the service has no endpoints, the health check does not block and readyz returns `ok` without delay.

I am seeing this behavior in 1.28.1 and 1.28.2, but not v1.27.6 or v1.27.5

### What did you expect to happen?

apiserver becomes ready without any additional delays

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy metrics-server to a Kubernetes cluster
2. Wait for api registration for `v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io` to complete (Available status is `true`).
3. Kill the kubelet and pods on the node hosting the metrics-server pod, such that the metrics-server service continues to show available endpoints, but the endpoint is 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by the AddUpdateAPIService function simultaneously adding and updating the APIService spec during startup, rather than deferring the spec update to be handled asynchronously by the controller. This synchronous update caused race conditions and health check blocking when discovery failed, leading to readiness delays.
FIX: Fix regression with adding aggregated apiservices panicking and affected health check introduced in release v1.28.0

TITLE: APIServices can be deleted at the apiserver startup
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Initially reported at 1.24.10, but it seems to be present in master as well:

We observe that a part of apiservices objects have been removed by "system:apiserver" right after the kubernetes upgrade.

It looks like there is race between "autoregister controller" [1] deleting apiservices and "crd-autoregister controller" populating a map of desired apiservices, i.e. in logs we see:
```
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070841Z Starting autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070858Z Waiting for caches to sync for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071116Z Starting crd-autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071128Z Waiting for caches to sync for crd-autoregister
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.270943Z Caches are synced for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.471323Z Caches are synced for crd-autoregister
```

The unwanted APIServices delete happened at 14:21:35.438 GMT so between crd-autoregister sync and autoregister controller.

It looks like we attempt to wait with "autoregister controller" for crd-autoregister to initialize here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5c1d2d4295f9b4eb12bfbf6429fdf989f2ca8a02
ROOT CAUSE: The server startup code incorrectly detects whether the CustomResourceDefinitions (CRD) API is enabled by checking the wrong condition or using improper logic. As a result, the autoregister controller proceeds to reconcile and delete APIService objects before the CRD controller has synced, causing a race condition where APIs for existing CRDs are mistakenly deleted at startup.
FIX: Fixes a bug at kube-apiserver start where APIService objects for custom resources could be deleted and recreated.
FILES: cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go, cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go, cmd/kube-apiserver/app/testing/testserver.go, test/integration/examples/apiserver_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The apiserver's admission webhook code incorrectly maps all non-Status webhook errors (including network errors such as timeouts, connection refusals, or broken pipes) to HTTP 400 Bad Request instead of a server error like 503 Service Unavailable. This happens because errors not wrapped inside a webhookutil.ErrCallingWebhook with a Status cause extractWebhookErrorWithStatus to unconditionally return a 400 Bad Request status, misleading clients about the nature of the failure and conflating network issues with client errors.

claims.text: The error handling function extractWebhookErrorWithStatus in staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/validating/dispatcher.go returns 400 Bad Request for all errors that do not wrap webhookutil.ErrCallingWebhook with a Status, including network errors, causing misleading HTTP codes on connection failures.

TITLE: APIServices can be deleted at the apiserver startup
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Initially reported at 1.24.10, but it seems to be present in master as well:

We observe that a part of apiservices objects have been removed by "system:apiserver" right after the kubernetes upgrade.

It looks like there is race between "autoregister controller" [1] deleting apiservices and "crd-autoregister controller" populating a map of desired apiservices, i.e. in logs we see:
```
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070841Z Starting autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070858Z Waiting for caches to sync for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071116Z Starting crd-autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071128Z Waiting for caches to sync for crd-autoregister
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.270943Z Caches are synced for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.471323Z Caches are synced for crd-autoregister
```

The unwanted APIServices delete happened at 14:21:35.438 GMT so between crd-autoregister sync and autoregister controller.

It looks like we attempt to wait with "autoregister controller" for crd-autoregister to initialize here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5c1d2d4295f9b4eb12bfbf6429fdf989f2ca8a02
ROOT CAUSE: The server startup code incorrectly detects whether the CustomResourceDefinitions (CRD) API is enabled by checking the wrong condition or using improper logic. As a result, the autoregister controller proceeds to reconcile and delete APIService objects before the CRD controller has synced, causing a race condition where APIs for existing CRDs are mistakenly deleted at startup.
FIX: Fixes a bug at kube-apiserver start where APIService objects for custom resources could be deleted and recreated.
FILES: cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go, cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go, cmd/kube-apiserver/app/testing/testserver.go, test/integration/examples/apiserver_test.go

TITLE: Request timeout not respected while listing from storage
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is possible to issue a list request which exceeds the duration set by the request-timeout apiserver flag. The request-timeout flag does not appear to be enforced when the apiserver is decoding the response from etcd. 

Specifically, listing a large number of CRDs from etcd can result in high request latency from using json encoding compared to protobuf encoding. While overall etcd latency is low, the overall listing from storage latency may be over the 1 minute timeout, particularly if the apiserver needs to fetch multiple pages from etcd.


### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the list requests to be subject to the duration specified by the request-timeout flag when this latency is coming from the listing from storage phase of the request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create 4000 CRs and list all the objects from etcd in 2 pages of 2000 objects. If the time to list 1 page + decode takes around 50s, listing 2 pages will result in the listing from storage phase of the request taking  around 1 minute and 40s before the request fails and the client is returned a 500 response code.

Logs for apiserver Tr
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the apiserver's request-timeout enforcement does not cover the duration spent decoding data fetched from etcd. When a large list request is served, the total time including multiple pages fetched and JSON decoding can exceed the timeout without being interrupted, resulting in request latency longer than configured. This is because the timeout mechanism only covers the etcd fetch phase but not the decoding phase.
FIX: Add apiserver.latency.k8s.io/decode-response-object annotation to the audit log to record the decoding time
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/request/webhook_duration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go

apiserver becomes ready without any additional delays

2. Wait for api registration for `v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io` to complete (Available status is `true`).
3. Kill the kubelet and pods on the node hosting the metrics-server pod, such that the metrics-server service continues to show available endpoints, but the endpoint is 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by the AddUpdateAPIService function simultaneously adding and updating the APIService spec during startup, rather than deferring the spec update to be handled asynchronously by the controller. This synchronous update caused race conditions and health check blocking when discovery failed, leading to readiness delays.

TITLE: kube-apiserver doesn't reload the kubelet client certificate/key on each logs query
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We bootstrap our clusters with kubeadm (through clusterapi), but provide our own end certs to shorten the certificate validity period.

Because of the shortened validity period, we rotate the file-based endcerts frequently. Recently we started noticing that after performing a certificate rotation, usage of `kubectl logs` was failing with

```sh
error: You must be logged in to the server (the server has asked for the client to provide credentials)
```

From there, we looked at the kube-apiserver and kubelet logs and found log lines like the following:

```
"Unable to authenticate the request due to an error" err="verifying certificate SN=<REMOVED>, SKID=<REMOVED>, AKID=<REMOVED> failed: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2022-12-17T02:31:09Z is after 2022-12-17T00:16:30Z"
```

So it looks like kube-apiserver didn't reload the new kubelet client certificate. This issue typically goes away if we restart the kube-apiserver container or continue to run `kubectl logs` in a loop.

### What did you expect to happen?

Being able to replace/rotate the kube-apiserver kubelet client certificate/key without causing failure for any 
ROOT CAUSE: The kube-apiserver did not reload or re-establish the TLS connections to the kubelet when the client certificate files used for authentication were rotated. Instead, it reused existing cached TLS connections which retained the old, expired certificates, causing authentication failures on subsequent requests such as 'kubectl logs'.
FIX: The Kubernetes API server now correctly detects and closes existing TLS connections when its client certificate file for kubelet authentication has been rotated.
FILES: cmd/kube-apiserver/app/options/options.go, cmd/kube-apiserver/app/options/options_test.go, pkg/kubelet/client/kubelet_client.go, pkg/kubelet/client/kubelet_client_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/cache.go, test/integration/apiserver/podlogs/podlogs_test.go

The minimum CPU request is not displayed in the pod status.

ROOT CAUSE: The bug happens because the Kubelet enforces a minimum CPU shares value (2m CPU) on Linux when the requested CPU resource is below that threshold or not specified. TITLE: HPA with container metrics fails when any pod is not in a ready state
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We've noticed that our HPA will stay at it's current scale and not make decisions when a pod is in an un-Ready state. IE a single pod is in CrashLoopBackoff and the HPA shows:

```
...
resource cpu of container "mycontainer" on pods  (as a percentage of request):     <unknown> / 50%
...
Warning  FailedGetResourceMetric  78s (x7 over 4m7s)  horizontal-pod-autoscaler  unable to get metric cpu: failed to get container metrics: container guides3 not present in metrics for pod namesapce/mycontainer-20240904t1338-433ca6a1-db998df74-s5rfh
```

That particular pod was in CrashLoopBackoff at the time and it wasn't until i removed it was it able to make scaling decisions

We're also running istio so there is another container in these pods and it's running ok; this may be why it's showing up in the metrics but unable to get info on the main container

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the HPA to ignore pods in this state and use only the Ready pods for its decisions

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Setup an HPA with container based metrics
Put one of the pods in bad state, could just have a single pod con
ROOT CAUSE: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) code prematurely fails and stops making scaling decisions if any pod's container metrics are missing, which can occur when a pod is not in a Ready state or a container is crashed or terminated. Instead of ignoring such pods, the HPA errors out, preventing scaling calculations from proceeding with the available valid pod metrics.
FIX: HPA's with ContainerResource metrics will no longer error when container metrics are missing, instead they will use the same logic Resource metrics are using to make calculations

TITLE: HPA metric got stuck at a random value and not scaling down after reaching max replica count
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I utilize two customized metrics, A and B, in my HPA system. A is a gauge-based metric called SLA Metric, while B is a count-based metric that tracks failed requests with HTTP status code 502 or 503 from Istio. These metrics are scraped by Prometheus.

To use custom metrics in HPA, we're employing Kube Metrics Adapter [link](https://github.com/zalando-incubator/kube-metrics-adapter). When the application load increases, the value of the SLA Metric also increases, and then the pods scale up until they reach the maximum replica count as expected.
However, the problem arises when the load dissipates, and the pods never scale down. Despite the SLA Metric's value being below the target in Prometheus, the HPA description still displays the metric value with a stale value that can be above or below the target.

One possible reason for this is that Metric B, which relies on Istio requests, shows up as unknown since there have been no failed requests with the 502 or 503 status codes. Thus, the Prometheus query fails.
We have noticed this behavior after upgrading Kube from version 1.21 to 1.24 and changing the HPA version from autoscaling/v2beta2 to autoscaling/v2
ROOT CAUSE: The HPA controller had an edge case where if a custom metric became unavailable (returned as unknown), the controller would not update the status metrics while updating the replica count. This caused the HPA to retain stale metric values and prevented scaling down even when the actual metric values fell below the target.
FIX: hpa: always update status metrics when updating the replica count
FILES: pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go

TITLE: Pod Garbage collector fails to clean up  PODs from nodes that are not running anymore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

This happened after upgrading to Kubernetes 1.26 from 1.24

The succession of events we have observed:
- Our workloads use HorizontalPodAutoscaler to scale up due to traffic increase
- Cluster Autoscaler provisions new nodes to accommodate the new replicas
- Traffic goes down
- HPA downsize replicas
- Cluster Autoscaler notices nodes under the threshold of usage and PODs can be accommodated into other nodes
- Nodes are drained and downscaled
- Kubernetes still reports PODs in a "Running" or "Terminating" state in the node that no longer exists
- Kubernetes control plane reports "Orphan pods" on its audit logs

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes Garbage collector to clean up these PODs after the node is gone

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy the following yaml deployments into a K8s cluster 1.26 and terminate one of the nodes

(duplicated port key "containerPort + protocol")
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: nginx
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: nginx
    app.kubernetes.io/component: deployment
spec:
  
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is a regression introduced by enabling PodDisruptionConditions by default. This caused the pod garbage collector to fail deleting pods that had duplicated fields such as repeated environment variable keys or container ports, resulting in orphan pods left on non-existent nodes. The garbage collector used Server-Side Apply (SSA) for patching Pod Disruption Conditions, which failed on pods with duplicated fields, blocking cleanup.
FIX: Fixed a regression in default configurations, which enabled PodDisruptionConditions by default, 
that prevented the control plane's pod garbage collector from deleting pods that contained duplicated field keys (env. variables with repeated keys or container ports).

TITLE: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the ClusterRole for service-account-issuer-discovery defines permissions for nonResourceURLs without trailing slashes, but the OpenAPI spec (swagger.json) documents these URLs with trailing slashes. This mismatch causes RBAC authorization to fail for legally formed requests that append a trailing slash, since the policy does not allow those exact paths.
FIX: Add slash ended urls for service-account-issuer-discovery to match API in swagger

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.

TITLE: Pod graceful deletion hangs if the kubelet already rejected that pod at admission time
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We observed the following series of events:

1) Pod is created with some attributes that later result in the pod being rejected at kubelet admission time
2) The pod is scheduled to a node
3) The pod is gracefully deleted by a controller, i.e. a deletion timestamp is set on the pod
4) The pod is rejected at kubelet admission time
5) The pod never gets deleted and is stuck: despite having the deletion timestamp set. It seems that kubelet does not issue the final force delete for the pod.

This is problematic in many scenarios, but one specific case it was hit was when the pod is backed by a daemonset controller. This issue manifested in way where since the pod never got deleted in step 5 above, the daemonset controller did not create a new pod to run the on the node and thus node was was not running a replica of the daemonset controller pod.

This seems to a be regression in k8s 1.27, I was not able to repro this behavior in 1.26.

### What did you expect to happen?

It is expected at during the series of events above, after the pod is failed at kubelet admission time, since the pod has a deletion timestamp set, the kubelet should forcefully delete
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because when a pod is rejected at kubelet admission time (such as due to an invalid nodeSelector), the kubelet does not proceed to delete the pod even if the pod has a deletion timestamp set. This results in the pod hanging in terminating state because the kubelet effectively ignores pods that were never fully admitted and thus never triggers the final deletion steps after kubelet restart.
FIX: Fix 1.27 regression with deletion of non-admissible pods that are deleted during Kubelet restart
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, test/e2e_node/restart_test.go

TITLE: Kubelet cannot finish terminating a pod that uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block` if the underlying block device is accidentally disconnected from the node
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A pod uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block`. The block volume is backed by a block device on the node (which is created by some CSI storage providers).  If the underlying block device corresponding to the volume is accidentally disconnected from the node (due to network, hardware problem, etc...), the user cannot delete the pod. The pod would be stuck in terminating forever since Kubelet refuses to unmount the block volume. This prevents the user from cleaning up the pod and spinning up a new replacement pod thus leading to a long service degradation. For example, if the pod is part of a statefulset, the replacement pod cannot come up due to the old pod being stuck terminating. 




### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should be able to finish terminating a pod when the corresponding block device is already removed from the node.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install a CSI storage provider that supports `volumeMode: Block`. For example, [Longhorn](https://github.com/longhorn/longhorn)
2. Deloy a statefulset that has volumeClaimTemplates with `volumeMode: Block`. For example:
    <details close>
  
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying block device backing the volume can have its sysfs backing_file path appended with a `(deleted)` suffix if the device is unexpectedly disconnected. The Kubelet code did not handle this suffix, causing it to fail to resolve the backing file path properly and consequently refuse to unmount the block device, which stuck the pod termination.
FIX: Trim out suffix added to backing file path of loopback device
FILES: pkg/volume/util/volumepathhandler/volume_path_handler_linux.go, pkg/volume/util/volumepathhandler/volume_path_handler_linux_test.go

TITLE: kubelet: PreStop Hooks can hang termination of a pod beyond pod's termination grace period
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Termination grace period includes the termination time of prestop hooks and containers in the pod. The total time that the pod terminates should always be < termination grace period seconds.

A misconfigured pod with a preStopHook that hangs indefinitely and pod ignoring SIGTERM can result in the pod taking 2X (double) the termination grace period seconds to terminate.
 

### What did you expect to happen?

The time to terminate the pod should always be <= termination grace period seconds including prestop hook execution time as documented in https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/#hook-handler-execution

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) Apply the following pod

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: prestop-repro
  labels:
    pod: prestop-repro
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 999999"]
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            ec
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying cause is that the kubelet allowed the preStop hook to run for the full terminationGracePeriodSeconds and only then started container termination, effectively allowing the pod termination to take up to twice the grace period. This behavior incorrectly extended the pod termination time beyond the specified grace period, contrary to the documented contract that the entire pod termination should complete within the grace period including preStop hooks.
FIX: Fixed the preStop hook will block the pod termination grace period
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go, test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The delay happens because processTaintBaseEviction uses the last observed ready condition of the node instead of the current ready condition to determine taint application. When a node becomes unreachable and its current ready condition switches to Unknown, the observed ready condition used is still True (last observed). This causes the NoExecute taint to be applied only after the next health monitoring cycle (approximately 5 seconds later) when the observed condition updates. Thus, using stale observedReadyCondition rather than the currentReadyCondition creates the unwanted 5-second delay in NoExecute taint addition.

claims.text: The function processTaintBaseEviction is called with observedReadyCondition, not currentReadyCondition, causing a delay when the current condition is Unknown but the observed condition is still True due to being stale.

This use of observedReadyCondition in processTaintBaseEviction leads to the NoExecute taint being added only after another monitorNodeHealth invocation updates observedReadyCondition, explaining the consistent 5s delay observed in the taint timestamp.

TITLE: APIServices can be deleted at the apiserver startup
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Initially reported at 1.24.10, but it seems to be present in master as well:

We observe that a part of apiservices objects have been removed by "system:apiserver" right after the kubernetes upgrade.

It looks like there is race between "autoregister controller" [1] deleting apiservices and "crd-autoregister controller" populating a map of desired apiservices, i.e. in logs we see:
```
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070841Z Starting autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070858Z Waiting for caches to sync for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071116Z Starting crd-autoregister controller

The unwanted APIServices delete happened at 14:21:35.438 GMT so between crd-autoregister sync and autoregister controller.

It looks like we attempt to wait with "autoregister controller" for crd-autoregister to initialize here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5c1d2d4295f9b4eb12bfbf6429fdf989f2ca8a02

TITLE: Kubectl restmapping cache causes inconsistent behaviour in case of resource name conflict
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I deployed a CRD (`teleportroles`) with the shortnames `role` and `roles`, conflicting with `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`.

Initially `kubectl get role` and `kubectl get roles` were both returnning `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

I ran `kubectl get teleportrole`.

Now, `kubectl get role` return my CRs instead of `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

However `kubectl get roles` continues to return `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect kubectl's behaviour to be consistent. The outcome of `kubectl get X` should not depend on the order the APIs were discovered and cached. I also expect exact names to be preferred over shortnames.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a freshly kubectl context (not one you already used and might have cached RESTMappings):
- create a CRD with a shortname conflicting with another resource, `role` for example
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the kube rbac resources are properly returned
- run `kubectl g
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that core Kubernetes resource types lacked singular names in their API discovery metadata, unlike CRDs. This omission caused the discovery client cache to prefer a CRD's shortname over the equivalent core resource singular name, leading to inconsistent RESTMapping resolution depending on the order resources were cached and fetched. Without singular names set for core types, the cache could be overwritten unpredictably when a CRD sharing a shortname was queried first.
FIX: Set singular names for core types to pass to discovery
