TITLE: Code Generation Produces Ambiguous Fields and Duplicate Methods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The changes introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121439 require that all types used with the generated clients implement both `runtime.Object` and `meta.Object`. In order to comply with this, we started embedding `metav1.ObjectMeta` in our API types that were missing it. However, we noticed that, for some of our types, the generator generates code with ambiguous fields and duplicate methods.

For example, consider the following case where both `metav1.ObjectMeta` and `MyEmbeddedType`, which are embedded in `MyType`, contain a `Namespace` field:

```


type MyType struct {
	metav1.TypeMeta   `json:",inline"`
	metav1.ObjectMeta `json:"metadata,omitempty"`

	MyEmbeddedType `json:"myEmbeddedType"`
}

type MyEmbeddedType struct {
	Namespace string `json:"namespace"`
}
```

This will generate code like:

```
func (b *MyTypeApplyConfiguration) WithNamespace(value string) *MyTypeApplyConfiguration {
	b.ensureObjectMetaApplyConfigurationExists()
	b.Namespace = &value
	return b
}
```

Here, `b.Namespace` is invalid because that field is present in both embedded types.



### What did you expect to happen?

Generat
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the code generator (applyconfiguration-gen) does not handle the presence of multiple embedded structs that contain fields with the same name. This leads the generator to produce methods and field accesses that are ambiguous or duplicated because it does not qualify or differentiate these fields based on their embedding types. The defect is that applyconfiguration-gen assumes unique member names at the top level without considering embedded struct conflicts.
FIX: applyconfiguration-gen no longer generates duplicate methods and ambiguous member accesses when types end up with multiple members of the same name (through embedded structs).

TITLE: Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L984-L1006
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L519-L543
4.  Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

```
Jul 25 1
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is a concurrency race in kubelet's device manager when allocating GPU devices to pods. The mutex guarding the allocated devices map is unlocked while calling out to device plugins, allowing concurrent updates and leading to inconsistent or nil map values. This causes the allocation function to panic due to nil map assignments when multiple GPU-using pods are created or deleted concurrently.
FIX: Fix kubelet panic when allocate resource for pod.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager_test.go

TITLE: kubectl apply requires CRDs to apply non-CRD resources if we use `kind: List`
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

kubectl apply performs validation before the apply. 

Non-CRD resources (e.g. pods / deployments) don't need CRD schema for validation, but if we use `kind: List` resource, kubectl calls `LIST apis/apiextensions.k8s.io/v1/customresourcedefinitions`.
In my Kubernetes cluster, administrator doesn't allow users to list CRDs, so user cannot apply non-CRD resources (e.g. pods / deployments) with `kind: List` resource.


### What did you expect to happen?

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  labels:
    app: nginx
  name: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  strategy: {}
  template:
    metadata:
      creationTimestamp: null
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged
        name: nginx-unprivileged
        resources: {}
status: {}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  labels:
    app: nginx2
  name: nginx2
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx2
  strategy: {}
  template:
    metadata:
      creationTimestamp: n
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying cause is that the OpenAPI schema used during kubectl apply validation does not include an entry for the 'List' resource kind. As a result, the validation logic treats 'List' kinds as CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs) and makes requests to the CRD API endpoint unnecessarily. This leads to issues when users lack permission to list CRDs, preventing them from applying non-CRD resources grouped in a 'List'.
FIX: Skip hasSupport check for List type

TITLE: Kubectl restmapping cache causes inconsistent behaviour in case of resource name conflict
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I deployed a CRD (`teleportroles`) with the shortnames `role` and `roles`, conflicting with `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`.

Initially `kubectl get role` and `kubectl get roles` were both returnning `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

I ran `kubectl get teleportrole`.

Now, `kubectl get role` return my CRs instead of `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

However `kubectl get roles` continues to return `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect kubectl's behaviour to be consistent. The outcome of `kubectl get X` should not depend on the order the APIs were discovered and cached. I also expect exact names to be preferred over shortnames.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a freshly kubectl context (not one you already used and might have cached RESTMappings):
- create a CRD with a shortname conflicting with another resource, `role` for example
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the kube rbac resources are properly returned
- run `kubectl g
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that core Kubernetes resource types lacked singular names in their API discovery metadata, unlike CRDs. This omission caused the discovery client cache to prefer a CRD's shortname over the equivalent core resource singular name, leading to inconsistent RESTMapping resolution depending on the order resources were cached and fetched. Without singular names set for core types, the cache could be overwritten unpredictably when a CRD sharing a shortname was queried first.
FIX: Set singular names for core types to pass to discovery

TITLE: Kubelet cannot finish terminating a pod that uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block` if the underlying block device is accidentally disconnected from the node
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A pod uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block`. The block volume is backed by a block device on the node (which is created by some CSI storage providers).  If the underlying block device corresponding to the volume is accidentally disconnected from the node (due to network, hardware problem, etc...), the user cannot delete the pod. The pod would be stuck in terminating forever since Kubelet refuses to unmount the block volume. This prevents the user from cleaning up the pod and spinning up a new replacement pod thus leading to a long service degradation. For example, if the pod is part of a statefulset, the replacement pod cannot come up due to the old pod being stuck terminating. 




### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should be able to finish terminating a pod when the corresponding block device is already removed from the node.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install a CSI storage provider that supports `volumeMode: Block`. For example, [Longhorn](https://github.com/longhorn/longhorn)
2. Deloy a statefulset that has volumeClaimTemplates with `volumeMode: Block`. For example:
    <details close>
  
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying block device backing the volume can have its sysfs backing_file path appended with a `(deleted)` suffix if the device is unexpectedly disconnected. The Kubelet code did not handle this suffix, causing it to fail to resolve the backing file path properly and consequently refuse to unmount the block device, which stuck the pod termination.
FIX: Trim out suffix added to backing file path of loopback device
FILES: pkg/volume/util/volumepathhandler/volume_path_handler_linux.go, pkg/volume/util/volumepathhandler/volume_path_handler_linux_test.go

TITLE: Can't restrict access from K8s nodes with loadBalancerSourceRanges for proxy-mode=ipvs
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When using loadBalancerSourceRanges to allow access only from CIDRs outside the cluster segment, access from the K8s nodes (or pods with hostNetwork:true) should be rejected, but for proxy-mode=ipvs it works.



### What did you expect to happen?

Access from K8s nodes should be rejected in the same way as for proxy-mode=iptables

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define a service with loadBalancerSourceRanges that allows access from a cidr outside the cluster, e.g.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: alpine
spec:
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
#  - "192.168.1.0/24"
  - "192.168.2.0/24"
#  - "fd00::c0a8:100/120"
  - "fd00::c0a8:200/120"
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  selector:
    app: alpine
  type: LoadBalancer
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  ports:
  - port: 5001
    name: nc
```
The K8s nodes have addresses on 192.168.1.0/24 and fd00::c0a8:100/120.

Make sure a loadBalancerIP is assigned (in this example 10.0.0.0/32) and try to access it from a K8s node:
```
# With proxy.mode=ipvs
> nc 10.0.0.0:5001
alpine-f6c8bd7db-zljnl    # (works)
# With proxy.mod
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the IPVS proxier was not correctly identifying the node ID when applying loadBalancerSourceRanges filtering, causing it to allow access from Kubernetes nodes that should have been rejected. Without the correct node ID, IPVS could not properly enforce source range restrictions, unlike iptables mode which handled them correctly.
FIX: Hardening LB SourceRanges filtering for IPVS proxier

TITLE: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue
ROOT CAUSE: The kube-proxy component lacked a properly configured --nodeport-addresses setting in a dual-stack environment, causing it to listen on all IP interfaces (0.0.0.0 and ::) by default. This results in healthCheckNodePort binding to all zeros (wildcard address) instead of a node's specific IP, because the code defaults to listening on all addresses if no specific nodeport address ranges are configured.
FIX: The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)

TITLE:  kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:
```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-LOAD-BALANCER dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-CLUSTER-IP dst,dst -j RETURN                                                                                                                                           
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable 
```
`KUBE-IPVS-IPS` seems to include external IPs (as al
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the iptables rule ordering in the KUBE-IPVS-FILTER chain wrongly rejected packets to healthCheckNodePorts on loadBalancer IPs, due to a restrictive rule introduced to reject new connections to IPVS IPs except for known service IPs. This rule blocked healthcheck traffic from GCP to the node ports for health checking, causing probes to fail. The healthCheckNodePort accept rule was missing in the iptables filter chain prior to the rejecting rule, causing legitimate healthcheck traffic to be dropped.
FIX: fixes 1.26 regression in kube-proxy ipvs accepting healthCheckNodePorts on the loadBalancerIP
FILES: pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go

TITLE: Document and test minimum privileges needed to run kube-proxy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running containers in privileged mode is not recommended as privileged containers run with all [linux capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html) enabled and can access the host's resources. Running containers in privileged mode opens number of security threads such as breakout to underlying host OS.

Currently the kube-proxy DaemonSet runs in privileged mode.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/863a462eeccca4c24bf4c4e9012f5ebccade70a2/cluster/addons/kube-proxy/kube-proxy-ds.yaml#L50-L51

https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy describes how to run kube-proxy in "rootless". To my understanding "rootless" != non-privileged mode but this configuration can be also used for running in non-privileged mode. However I see that following issues with it:
1. In the provided kube-proxy component config in https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy we have to disable certain settins to prevent kube-proxy from ensuring sysctls (which is allowed only in privileged container).

But when I tried to run kube-proxy with the prov
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because kube-proxy requires setting certain sysctls that need privileged container mode, but there was no mechanism to run these privileged operations separately from the main non-privileged kube-proxy process. This forced kube-proxy to run fully privileged or fail when run with lowered privileges, with no way to disable these sysctl settings via configuration.
FIX: Added a new `--init-only` command line flag to `kube-proxy`. Setting the flag makes `kube-proxy` perform its initial configuration that requires privileged mode, and then exit. The `--init-only` mode is intended to be executed in a privileged init container, so that the main container may run with a stricter `securityContext`.

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Scheduler should use max(Spec.Resources.Requests, Status.Resources.Requests) instead of Status.AllocatedResources
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Current implementation of in-place pod resize looks at max(Spec.Resources, Status.Resources) which works well when resources are being increased, and works well when resources are being decreased assuming that the decrease request is based on observed lower usage, and the new lowered resources does not exceed current usage.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d86b74b0176c6fa22ba2559ace961fa25c6e98cf/pkg/api/v1/resource/helpers.go#L64-L73

However, a bad actor can game the system by requesting resize to resources lower than current usage, and kubelet grants it not knowing that runtime cannot enforce it, and scheduler may schedule pods to an oversubscribed node. A simple way to avoid this is to use Status.Resources.Requests instead of Status.AllocatedResources.

This also means that containerd and other runtimes need to be at a version that supports the feature so that users get the correct signals (avoid 'forever InProgress')


### What did you expect to happen?

When desired resources are lowered and kubelet admits it and sets status to InProgress, scheduler should schedule new pods against resources that are actually available. Bad actors sho
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler made scheduling decisions based on the max of requested and status resources without considering that the kubelet might have admitted a decrease below current actual usage. This allowed pods to be resized to resource amounts lower than what the runtime could enforce, causing potential oversubscription and incorrect scheduling.
FIX: ContainerStatus.AllocatedResources is now guarded by a separate feature gate, InPlacePodVerticalSaclingAllocatedStatus
FILES: pkg/api/pod/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util_test.go, pkg/features/kube_features.go, pkg/features/versioned_kube_features.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/helpers_linux.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/quota/v1/evaluator/core/pods.go, pkg/quota/v1/evaluator/core/pods_test.go

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Minimum CPU request is displayed when only memory request is configured
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` is enabled and only a memory resource request is configured in a pod, the minimum CPU request set internally is displayed in the pod status:
```
$ kubectl get pod testpod -o jsonpath='spec: {.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\nallocatedResources: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].allocatedResources}{"\nstatus: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].resources}{"\n"}'
spec: {"requests":{"memory":"200Mi"}}
allocatedResources: {"memory":"200Mi"}
status: {"requests":{"cpu":"2m","memory":"200Mi"}}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The minimum CPU request is not displayed in the pod status.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enables the `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` feature.
2. Create a pod where only memory request is configured:
   <Details>

   ```
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod
   metadata:
     labels:
       run: testpod
     name: testpod
   spec:
     containers:
     - image: nginx
       name: testpod
       resources:
         requests:
           memory: 200Mi
     restartPolicy: Always
   ```

   </Details>
3. See its resources in the pod status:
   ```
   $ ku
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happens because the Kubelet enforces a minimum CPU shares value (2m CPU) on Linux when the requested CPU resource is below that threshold or not specified. This leads to the pod status showing a minimum CPU request that was not originally specified in the pod spec, causing confusion and mismatch in resource reporting when only memory requests are configured.
FIX: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Handle edge cases around CPU MinShares

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Resizing pod gets stuck if limit is not configured
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Resizing CPU requests gets stuck in `InProgress` if the CPU limit is not configured:
```
$ kubectl patch pod resize-pod --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"resize-container", "resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"300m"}}}]}}'
pod/resize-pod patched
$ sleep 300
$ kubectl get pod resize-pod -o jsonpath='spec: {.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\nallocatedResources: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].allocatedResources}{"\nstatus: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].resources}{"\nresize: "}{.status.resize}{"\n"}'
spec: {"requests":{"cpu":"300m","memory":"200Mi"}}
allocatedResources: {"cpu":"300m","memory":"200Mi"}
status: {"requests":{"cpu":"200m","memory":"200Mi"}}
resize: InProgress
```

The internal behavior in kubelet varies depending on other resource limits configuration.
- If the limit for another resource is also not configured, no action is computed at `computePodResizeAction()`:
  ```
  Jul 26 13:43:09 kind-control-plane kubelet[708]: I0726 13:43:09.494698     708 kuberuntime_manager.go:1051] "computePodActions got for pod" podActions="KillPod: false, CreateSandbox: false, UpdatePodResources: false, Attempt: 0, InitContainersToStart: [], Containers
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the pod resizing logic in kubelet did not account for containers without resource limits set. Specifically, the code assumed CPU limits were always present, causing failure or no action when limits were missing. This led to resize operations getting stuck in an 'InProgress' state because the code failed to compute or apply resize actions properly without limits information.
FIX: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Enable resizing containers without limits

TITLE: removeMissingExtendedResources() did not remove unknown extension resources from InitContainer
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The function removeMissingExtendedResources() located at pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/predicate.go:217, is designed to remove any extended resources from a container’s requests that are not found in nodeInfo.Allocatable before the pod is admitted. This is necessary to support cluster-level resources, which are extended resources that are unknown to nodes.
However, this function only removes missingExtendedResources from the container’s requests, and does not process the requests of initContainers. This could lead to issues, as initContainers might request resources that do not exist on the node, which could result in the pod failing to be admitted or other unforeseen issues. As such, it may be necessary to refine the removeMissingExtendedResources() function to also handle initContainer’s requests.

### What did you expect to happen?

Refine the removeMissingExtendedResources() function to also handle initContainer’s requests.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod that requests cluster-level extended resources in both the container and InitContainer.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes versi
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the removeMissingExtendedResources() function was incomplete in its processing scope; it only sanitized the extended resource requests of regular containers but neglected to perform the same cleanup for initContainers. Since initContainers can also request extended resources unknown to the node, this omission led to potential resource mismatches and pod admission failures.
FIX: Remove missing extended resources from init containers
FILES: pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/predicate.go, pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/predicate_test.go

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that when a Pod has its spec.nodeName field set (indicating it is pre-assigned to a specific node), the Dynamic Resources scheduler plugin is bypassed and does not run. Since this plugin is responsible for managing resource claims and reservations, bypassing it leads to the pod being rejected or failing to run because its resource claims are not properly allocated or reserved. This limitation arises because the scheduler plugin is skipped when the pod is pre-scheduled, preventing the dynamic resource allocation logic from executing.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller_test.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/controller_policy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/controller/controller.go, test/e2e/dra/dra.go, test/e2e/dra/test-driver/app/controller.go, test/integration/util/util.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the pod-level resource request validation logic incorrectly assumes that if a resource is not specified at the pod level, its request defaults to zero. This leads to a validation error when container-level requests for that resource exist and are aggregated, since zero is treated as less than the containers' aggregate. The validation should instead only compare pod-level and container-level requests for resources explicitly set at the pod level, skipping those absent in pod.spec.resources.requests.

claims.text: The validation code initially fetched the pod-level resource request by assuming it always exists, defaulting to zero if missing, causing failure when container requests aggregated to more than zero for that resource.
The fix adds a presence check on the pod-level resource request map before comparison to skip validating resources not set at pod-level, preventing erroneous zero-default validation errors.
The observed symptom of 'Invalid value: "0": must be >= aggregate container requests' matches this logic error of treating missing pod-level resource requests as zero rather than skipping validation.

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The control plane comes up just fine but then when you try to create a k8s service, it fails due to a broken behavior with the IP Allocator

Since this is not really a supported version of the k8s, I went around digging up a bit more to see what is the regular behavior and found this to be very inconsistent across a few release branches.

ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the IP allocator code uses big.Int to represent IP addresses for arithmetic. However, when converting from big.Int back to IP byte arrays, the implementation only took the minimal byte slice from big.Int, which omits leading zero bytes. diagnosis.root_cause: When creating an already existing service, the IPAddress resource for the service's ClusterIP is created but its ParentReference does not match the service's actual references, triggering the repairip controller to detect this mismatch as a 'wrong reference'. This causes the controller to emit a warning event and delete the IPAddress, resulting in the IP address being cleaned up unnecessarily. This behavior occurs because the operator creating the Service does not check for existence and ignores "Already Exists" errors, and the repairip controller strictly validates the IPAddress parent references. Thus, the defect is in the logic that enforces this strict ParentReference validation leading to event spam and resource churn when multiple identical Service creation requests occur.

claims.text: The repairip.go code logs a warning event and deletes the IPAddress resource if the IPAddress's ParentReference does not match the Service's ClusterIPs, which causes new IPAddresses to be created then cleaned up on repeated creation requests for the same Service.

The observed repeated warning events and IPAddress deletion errors match the behavior of repairip.go handling "wrong reference" IPAddresses, explaining why creating an existing Service causes IP addresses to be created and cleaned up unnecessarily.
Operator code that creates Services without existence checks leads to repeated creation attempts triggering this IPAddress cleanup logic, causing event spam but no further errors.

TITLE: CEL validation can cause APIServer to crashloop
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We observed a scenario that can cause APIServer to crash due to a CEL validation issue for CRD.
There's an edge case that when a CRD schema is updated after a CR instance is created, CRD finalizer can cause APIServer to crash when the CRD is being deleted.
Updating the CRD schema after some CRs are created can be problematic, but it should fail gracefully instead of crash.

<details>

Sample stack trace
</summary>

```

panic({0x42d7a80?, 0x7a07d50?})

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, chec
ROOT CAUSE: The volume_manager's podWorker calls WaitForUnmount asynchronously. If the final asynchronous call happens after the populator has cleaned up its resources, a pod UID is added to the processedPods map but the populator no longer tracks that pod. This pod entry then remains in processedPods indefinitely because the cleanup code only processes pods currently tracked by the volume_manager's internal cache.
FIX: Fix memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

diagnosis.root_cause: The kubelet podresources List API defect arises because it uses a pod provider method that returns all pods including terminated ones, instead of filtering for only active pods as resource managers do. This leads the endpoint to report stale resource allocations for terminated pods, especially for memory resources where no explicit sync occurs to clean stale data. The inconsistency between the pod set used by the List API (all pods) and the pod set used by resource managers (active pods) causes this incorrect reporting.

claims.text: The List API implementation uses p.podsProvider.GetPods() which returns all pods, including terminated pods, not just active ones. Thus, the endpoint reports resource allocations for terminated pods incorrectly.
Resource managers use only active pods when tracking resource allocations, causing a discrepancy between what the List API returns and the actual resource allocation state.

Unlike device resources, CPU and memory resource managers do not have explicit synchronization to clean stale allocations promptly, so stale memory assignments of terminated pods persist and are incorrectly reported.

TITLE: windows cpu maximum incorrect with more than one processor group
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When submitting a windows pod using resource limits on a node with more than one processor group, the specified `CpuMaximum` count is incorrect due to the usage of `runtime.NumCPU()` which does not take processor groups into account.

For example:
- node with 96 cores
- cpu limit 94
- `runtime.NumCPU()` returns `48`

This results in a CPU maximum of 10000 since the range is from [1, 10000]:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_windows.go#L82..L91

```go
	limit := int64(94 * 1000)
	numCPU := 48
	fmt.Println(((10000 * limit) / int64(numCPU) / 1000))


```

Our initial goal for this was to limit a process to not use all available CPU and therefore render the node uncontrollable. 

### What did you expect to happen?

A CPU maximum of `9791` instead of `10000` for that specific case. For the calculation, it should use the CPU count for all available processor groups instead of just the current one. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Launch a node with a lot of CPUs, for example [a Azure Standard_D96a_v4](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azur
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused because the code incorrectly used `runtime.NumCPU()` to determine the number of logical CPUs on Windows nodes. This function only returns the number of processors in the current processor group and does not aggregate CPU counts across multiple processor groups, leading to an underestimated CPU count when nodes have more than 64 logical processors. This incorrect CPU count causes the CPU maximum calculation to be incorrect for such nodes.
FIX: Fixed an issue when calculating CPU limits on Windows nodes with more than 64 logical processors
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_windows.go, pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_windows_test.go, pkg/kubelet/winstats/perfcounter_nodestats.go

Status of pods can become "OutOfCpu" when many pods are created and completed in a short time on the same node.

### What did you expect to happen?

Status of pods should become "Running", "Pending" or "Completed".

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I created a procedure to reproduce this state.
https://gist.github.com/shioshiota/84f1f4e162c335fe551c60a118676c3c

### Anything else we need to know?

We couldn't reproduce this behavior in kubernetes 1.21.2 cluster.
We found this issue in kubernetes 1.22.4.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"21", GitVersion:"v1.21.3", GitCommit:"ca643a4d1f7bfe34773c74f79527be4afd95bf39", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-07-15T21:04:39Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.6", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.4", GitCommit:"b695d79d4f967c403a96986f1750a35eb75e75f1", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-11-23T01:42:25Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.10", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/arm64"}
```

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>
no
</details>


ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Kubelet prematurely marked pods as terminated (Succeeded or Failed) in the API before all containers were fully stopped and prevented from restarting. This caused rapid repurposing of node resources and led to inaccurate 'OutOfCpu' errors on subsequent pods, due to resource accounting being inconsistent during quick pod turnover.
FIX: Fixed a 1.22 regression that could incorrectly reject pods with OutOfCpu errors if they were rapidly scheduled after other pods were reported as complete in the API. The Kubelet now waits to report the phase of a pod as terminal in the API until all running containers are guaranteed to have stopped and no new containers can be started.  Short-lived pods may take slightly longer (~1s) to report Succeeded or Failed after this change.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug is caused by the integer division of the requested number of CPUs by CPUsPerCore in the takePartialUncore method. When the requested CPUs count is odd and SMT is enabled (CPUsPerCore=2), numCoresNeeded is calculated as the floor division (rounded down), causing the allocation logic to request fewer cores than actually needed and fail the claim check that requires exact matching requested CPUs. Consequently, no CPUs are allocated aligned to the uncore cache, and the fallback allocates CPUs not aligned as intended, effectively disabling the 'prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache' policy for odd CPU counts under SMT.

claims.text: The allocation method takePartialUncore calculates numCoresNeeded using integer division of numCPUsNeeded by CPUsPerCore(), which causes truncation when numCPUsNeeded is odd and CPUsPerCore is 2 (SMT enabled).

This truncated numCoresNeeded results in claim being false for odd CPU requests since claimed requires exact match of requested CPUs with free CPUs found in the selected cores, causing no CPUs to be allocated aligned to the uncore cache.
The fallback behavior when claim is false leads to allocation of CPUs not aligned by uncore cache, so the 'prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache' option is effectively not honored for odd CPU counts.

TITLE:  kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:
```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-LOAD-BALANCER dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-CLUSTER-IP dst,dst -j RETURN                                                                                                                                           
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable 
```
`KUBE-IPVS-IPS` seems to include external IPs (as al
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the iptables rule ordering in the KUBE-IPVS-FILTER chain wrongly rejected packets to healthCheckNodePorts on loadBalancer IPs, due to a restrictive rule introduced to reject new connections to IPVS IPs except for known service IPs. This rule blocked healthcheck traffic from GCP to the node ports for health checking, causing probes to fail. The healthCheckNodePort accept rule was missing in the iptables filter chain prior to the rejecting rule, causing legitimate healthcheck traffic to be dropped.
FIX: fixes 1.26 regression in kube-proxy ipvs accepting healthCheckNodePorts on the loadBalancerIP
FILES: pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go

TITLE: Can't restrict access from K8s nodes with loadBalancerSourceRanges for proxy-mode=ipvs
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When using loadBalancerSourceRanges to allow access only from CIDRs outside the cluster segment, access from the K8s nodes (or pods with hostNetwork:true) should be rejected, but for proxy-mode=ipvs it works.



### What did you expect to happen?

Access from K8s nodes should be rejected in the same way as for proxy-mode=iptables

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define a service with loadBalancerSourceRanges that allows access from a cidr outside the cluster, e.g.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: alpine
spec:
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
#  - "192.168.1.0/24"
  - "192.168.2.0/24"
#  - "fd00::c0a8:100/120"
  - "fd00::c0a8:200/120"
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  selector:
    app: alpine
  type: LoadBalancer
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  ports:
  - port: 5001
    name: nc
```
The K8s nodes have addresses on 192.168.1.0/24 and fd00::c0a8:100/120.

Make sure a loadBalancerIP is assigned (in this example 10.0.0.0/32) and try to access it from a K8s node:
```
# With proxy.mode=ipvs
> nc 10.0.0.0:5001
alpine-f6c8bd7db-zljnl    # (works)
# With proxy.mod
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the IPVS proxier was not correctly identifying the node ID when applying loadBalancerSourceRanges filtering, causing it to allow access from Kubernetes nodes that should have been rejected. Without the correct node ID, IPVS could not properly enforce source range restrictions, unlike iptables mode which handled them correctly.
FIX: Hardening LB SourceRanges filtering for IPVS proxier
FILES: pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier_test.go

TITLE: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersRe
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. Since the change trackers use their own mutexes independent from the proxier's, a new event could be processed between these calls, leading to inconsistent state and some endpoint updates being missed.
FIX: Fixes a race condition in the iptables mode of kube-proxy in 1.27 and later
that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a
new endpoint, the rules for the new endpoint might not be added until
much later).
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/endpointslicecache.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/service.go, pkg/proxy/service_test.go

TITLE: kube-proxy nftables mode failed to delete rules due to "Device or resource busy" consistently in some cases
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

While validating nftable mode using conformance test, the following error logs were produced consistently:
```
E0104 17:21:56.957351       1 proxier.go:941] "Unable to delete stale chains; will retry later" err=<
        /dev/stdin:1:28-90: Error: Could not process rule: Device or resource busy
        delete chain ip kube-proxy service-QZNVUP4F-endpointslice-3291/example-named-port/tcp/http
                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
        /dev/stdin:3:28-109: Error: Could not process rule: Device or resource busy
        delete chain ip kube-proxy endpoint-A6Z5NSSV-endpointslice-3291/example-named-port/tcp/http__10.244.2.28/3001
                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

I0104 18:43:05.900199       1 proxier.go:935] "Deleting stale nftables chains" numChains=1
E0104 18:43:05.945300       1 proxier.go:941] "Unable to delete stale chains; will retry later" err=<
        /dev/stdin:1:28-93: Error: Could not process rule: Device or resource busy
        delete chain ip kube-proxy endpoint-EVHUKXWZ-services-4440/externa
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because a chain that was once identified as stale and added to the staleChains set could subsequently become active again. However, the proxier does not remove such chains from staleChains when they become active. Consequently, the proxier attempts to delete these chains even though they are currently active, causing errors indicating "Device or resource busy". The proxier's failure to update staleChains to reflect the chain's active status causes invalid deletion attempts.
FIX: kube-proxy: do not delete previously stale but currently active chains

diagnosis.root_cause: The kube-proxy nftables implementation creates drop rules in the 'no-endpoint-services' map for services with externalTrafficPolicy=Local that currently have no local endpoints, and installs these rules in a chain executed at a filter OUTPUT hook with lower priority than DNAT. Consequently, traffic from pods targeting external IPs of such services is prematurely dropped before being DNATed to endpoints, causing blackholing. Attempts to fix by adjusting match criteria failed due to nftables data-type constraints.

claims.text: The nftables proxier sets up a vmap 'no-endpoint-services' that matches destination IP, protocol, and port to drop traffic to services without endpoints, which causes traffic to external IPs of LoadBalancer services with externalTrafficPolicy=Local to be dropped.

TITLE: Status manager does not normalize ephemeral container statuses
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

`EphemeralContainerStatuses` is not normalized in 	`normalizeStatus()` in the status manager:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L1026-L1043

This does not seem to cause any user facing problem because `EphemeralContainerStatuses` is sorted before passed to the status manager and timestamps are normalized at marshaling to create a patch:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2336

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L873

However, an unexpected behavior is caused internally because timestamps are not normalized. If the log verbosity is 3 or larger, the following messages are logged periodically in kubelet when an ephemeral container exists:

```
May 14 20:10:33 kind-control-plane kubelet[720]: I0514 20:10:33.437155 	720 status_manager.go:230] "Syncing all statuses"
May 14 20:10:33 kind-control-plane kubelet[720]: I0514 20:10:33.438512 	720 status_manager.go:984] "Pod status is inconsistent with cache
ROOT CAUSE: The status manager failed to apply normalization logic to EphemeralContainerStatuses when processing pod status updates. This omission caused minor timestamp differences to persist, leading the kubelet to believe pod status was inconsistent and triggering continual unnecessary synchronization attempts.
FIX: normalize ephemeral container statuses
FILES: pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs due to a race condition between the creation of streams and their consumption in concurrent goroutines. Specifically, the readDemuxLoop goroutine attempts to retrieve a stream by its ID before the stream has been created by the stream function, leading to a nil stream and the logged error 'Unknown stream id N, discarding message'. This happens because the readDemuxLoop and stream are running concurrently without synchronization, so the order of stream creation and consumption is not guaranteed.

claims.text: The readDemuxLoop runs in a separate goroutine concurrently with the stream function that creates streams, leading to potential timing issues on stream creation and retrieval.

When readDemuxLoop tries to get a stream by ID before the stream is created, it logs the error 'Unknown stream id N, discarding message', indicating a race where getStream is called before CreateStream.

TITLE: kubelet: Process Stats are always 0 as returned by kubelet summary API 
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

[Process stats](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/stats/v1alpha1#ProcessStats) are not currently returned in kubelet summary API.



### What did you expect to happen?

[Process stats](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/stats/v1alpha1#ProcessStats) are returned correctly in kubelet summary API.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start a cluster (using kind cluster from master)

```
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                 STATUS   ROLES           AGE     VERSION
kind-control-plane   Ready    control-plane   7m49s   v1.27.0-alpha.0.1120+56a14025b06734
kind-worker          Ready    <none>          7m27s   v1.27.0-alpha.0.1120+56a14025b06734
```

3. Launch a pod and consume a few pids, e.g. 10 pids
4. Fetch summary api and examine the process stats

```
$ kubectl run -i --tty --rm debug --image=k8s.gcr.io/busybox:latest --restart=Never -- /bin/sh
/ # for i in $(seq 1 10); do sleep 99999999 & done
/ # ps aux
PID   USER     COMMAND
    1 root     /bin/sh
   16 root     sleep 99999999
   17 root     sleep 99999999
   18 root     sleep 99999999
   19 root     sleep 99999999
 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Kubelet's eviction logic and stats providers did not properly calculate or report process counts (PIDs) for pods. This caused the process stats to always show zero in the summary API, which is why process-based eviction never triggered. The underlying defect was incomplete or incorrect integration of process counting from cAdvisor and CRI stats providers into the Kubelet's eviction subsystem and Metrics API.
FIX: Fix a bug where the Kubelet didn't calculate the process usage of pods correctly, leading to pods never getting evicted for PID use.

TITLE: kubelet: Evicted and force deleted pods get their full termination grace period when they should not
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When pods are evicted, i.e. with a hard eviction, the grace period is intended to be `0s` (i.e. do not respect the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). 

However, currently, evicted pods receive their full termination grace period seconds.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod is evicted immediately and the termination grace period is not respected 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the following pod which has an ephemeral storage limit of 5Mi and uses `dd` to fill the disk

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: evictdiskpod
  labels:
    pod: evictdiskpod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: 5Mi
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        sleep 10
        dd if=/dev/zero of=file bs=1M count=10
        echo 'write done'
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because a grace period override of 0 was used during eviction to force immediate pod termination, but the pod worker logic interpreted a zero override as no override and used the pod's full configured grace period. This caused evicted and force deleted pods to respect their full termination grace period instead of being terminated immediately. To enforce immediate eviction, a grace period override of 1 second must be used instead of zero.
FIX: Fixes a bug where hard evictions due to resource pressure would let the pod have the full termination grace period, instead of shutting down instantly. This bug also affected force deleted pods. Both cases now get a termination grace period of 1 second.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/eviction/helpers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that when a Pod has its spec.nodeName field set (indicating it is pre-assigned to a specific node), the Dynamic Resources scheduler plugin is bypassed and does not run. Since this plugin is responsible for managing resource claims and reservations, bypassing it leads to the pod being rejected or failing to run because its resource claims are not properly allocated or reserved. This limitation arises because the scheduler plugin is skipped when the pod is pre-scheduled, preventing the dynamic resource allocation logic from executing.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller_test.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/controller_policy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/controller/controller.go, test/e2e/dra/dra.go, test/e2e/dra/test-driver/app/controller.go, test/integration/util/util.go

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

TITLE: scheduler: data race between PodInfo.Update and PriorityQueue.AddNominatedPod
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

As part of adding support for dynamic resource allocation to `test/integration/scheduler_perf`, I ran `go test -race`. With DRA, scheduling failures occur, and that led to a race report:

```
$ go test -v -timeout=0 -bench=.*/SchedulingWithInlineResourceClaims/ -race ./test/integration/scheduler_perf

WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at 0x00c000baafc0 by goroutine 25750:
  k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/framework.(*PodInfo).Update()
      /nvme/gopath/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go:216 +0xd2e
  k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue.updatePod()
      /nvme/gopath/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go:903 +0x5a4
  k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue.(*PriorityQueue).Update()
      /nvme/gopath/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go:620 +0x582
  k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler.(*Scheduler).updatePodInSchedulingQueue()
      /nvme/gopath/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go:140 +0x359
  k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler.(*Scheduler).updatePodInSchedulingQueue-fm()
      <autogenerated>:1 +0x6d
  k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache.ResourceE
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the PodNominator and the SchedulingQueue used separate locks to protect access to the same `*QueuedPodInfo` objects. When one goroutine updated a PodInfo while another simultaneously accessed it via a different lock, a data race happened. The issue was that the locking was not shared, which led to concurrent unsynchronized access.
FIX: Fixed data race in `kube-scheduler` when preemption races with a Pod update.
FILES: pkg/scheduler/framework/interface.go, pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go, pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go, pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue_test.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The PodResourcesAPI's List() method directly retrieves pods via podsProvider.GetPods() and reports resources for all pods including those in terminal phases (Succeeded or Failed) without filtering them out. This causes resources of pods which have completed their lifecycle to be reported as currently in use, even though resource managers internally consider them available for reassignment. TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

TITLE: StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` should create pods in parallel
SYMPTOM: ### What would you like to be added?

When `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` is set, StatefulSetController should issue create requests for replicas in batches (similar to how other controllers work, e.g. ReplicaSetController) when creating pods for the first time and scaling up.

### Why is this needed?

Currently even with `Parallel` podManagementPolicy StatefulSet the replicas are still _created_ sequentially, even though they can start to _run_ in any order.

This severely limits pod throughput when working with large StatefulSets (~thousands of replicas). For example, 10 StatefulSets with 5k pods each achieve a total of ~6 pods/s, while 1k StatefulSets with 50 pods each allows for creating ~120 pods/s. 

`Parallel` policy suggests the pods can be created sequentially (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/stateful-set-v1/#StatefulSetSpec): 

>The alternative policy is Parallel which will create pods in parallel to match the desired scale without waiting, and on scale down will delete all pods at once.

Relevant code (`Parallel` policy controls the value of `monotonic`): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/s
ROOT CAUSE: The StatefulSet controller's implementation incorrectly creates pods sequentially even when the `podManagementPolicy` is set to `Parallel`. This goes against the policy's intention that pods can be created concurrently, resulting in performance bottlenecks for large StatefulSets due to unnecessary serialization of pod creation requests.
FIX: Faster StatefulSet creation when `Parallel` mode is enabled.
FILES: pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go, pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control_test.go, pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_utils.go

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, chec
ROOT CAUSE: The volume_manager's podWorker calls WaitForUnmount asynchronously. If the final asynchronous call happens after the populator has cleaned up its resources, a pod UID is added to the processedPods map but the populator no longer tracks that pod. This pod entry then remains in processedPods indefinitely because the cleanup code only processes pods currently tracked by the volume_manager's internal cache.

diagnosis.root_cause: The StatefulSet controller's update process only enforces the minReadySeconds wait period if the podManagementPolicy is set to OrderedReady (monotonic=true). When podManagementPolicy is Parallel (monotonic=false), the code does not apply the minReadySeconds delay and immediately proceeds to upgrade the next pod as soon as it becomes ready, leading to the observed ignoring of minReadySeconds.

claims.text: The update process in StatefulSet controller uses a 'monotonic' boolean flag which is true for podManagementPolicy=OrderedReady and false for Parallel; the minReadySeconds readiness wait is only enforced when monotonic is true.
This design causes the minReadySeconds delay to be ignored for podManagementPolicy=Parallel, explaining why rollout updates do not wait for the minReadySeconds after pod readiness in Parallel mode.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug is caused by the StatefulSet controller's scale down logic that blocks termination of pods when they are not both running and available (Ready and minReadySeconds passed). Specifically, the controller identifies the first unhealthy pod and prevents any other pod from scaling down until that pod becomes available, but the availability check is scheduled asynchronously with minReadySeconds delay and can be dropped if a prior check is pending. This leads to a sync stall where the pod to be terminated is never recognized as available and the scale down does not proceed until a full kube-controller-manager resync occurs, which can be very delayed.

claims.text: The processCondemned function in stateful_set_control.go blocks scale down if a pod is not running and ready and is not the first unhealthy pod, causing delay in pod termination until the first unhealthy pod becomes available.

The updateStatefulSet function partitions pods and uses firstUnhealthyPod to block terminating pods, which matches the observed stall until the first unhealthy pod is available or a full resync happens.

The StatefulSet controller schedules delayed re-enqueue of the StatefulSet after minReadySeconds to check pod availability, but if a prior scheduling exists the new event is discarded, causing delays in availability evaluation and blocking scale down.

This gap allows the GC to delete objects like DaemonSets despite them having a valid updated ownerReference.

This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersRe
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. Since the change trackers use their own mutexes independent from the proxier's, a new event could be processed between these calls, leading to inconsistent state and some endpoint updates being missed.
FIX: Fixes a race condition in the iptables mode of kube-proxy in 1.27 and later
that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a
new endpoint, the rules for the new endpoint might not be added until
much later).

TITLE:  kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:
```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-LOAD-BALANCER dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-CLUSTER-IP dst,dst -j RETURN                                                                                                                                           
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable 
```
`KUBE-IPVS-IPS` seems to include external IPs (as al
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the iptables rule ordering in the KUBE-IPVS-FILTER chain wrongly rejected packets to healthCheckNodePorts on loadBalancer IPs, due to a restrictive rule introduced to reject new connections to IPVS IPs except for known service IPs. This rule blocked healthcheck traffic from GCP to the node ports for health checking, causing probes to fail. The healthCheckNodePort accept rule was missing in the iptables filter chain prior to the rejecting rule, causing legitimate healthcheck traffic to be dropped.
FIX: fixes 1.26 regression in kube-proxy ipvs accepting healthCheckNodePorts on the loadBalancerIP

TITLE: kube-proxy fails to start for IPv6 when underlying infra is dual stack in 1.28
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A new  kube-proxyvalidation introduced in k8s 1.28 seems to break Azure + ipv6. IPv6 clusters on Azure run on dual-stack hosts. The IPv6 node IP seems like it's only getting assigned to the Node until after kube-proxy starts (someone might need to help me understand what component is responsible). However, kube-proxy now fails to start with:

kube-proxy is in CrashloopBackoff, logs show:

``` 
I0825 16:18:19.872382       1 server_others.go:69] "Using iptables proxy"
I0825 16:18:19.892673       1 node.go:141] Successfully retrieved node IP: 10.1.0.6
I0825 16:18:19.894163       1 conntrack.go:52] "Setting nf_conntrack_max" nfConntrackMax=131072

E0825 16:18:19.912228       1 server.go:537] "Error running ProxyServer" err="kube-proxy configuration is incorrect: cluster is IPv4-primary but clusterCIDRs contains only IPv6 addresses"
E0825 16:18:19.912240       1 run.go:74] "command failed" err="kube-proxy configuration is incorrect: cluster is IPv4-primary but clusterCIDRs contains only IPv6 addresses"
```

FIX: Fixed a regression in kube-proxy where it might refuse to start if given
single-stack IPv6 configuration options on a node that has both IPv4 and
IPv6 IPs.

TITLE: Document and test minimum privileges needed to run kube-proxy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running containers in privileged mode is not recommended as privileged containers run with all [linux capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html) enabled and can access the host's resources. Running containers in privileged mode opens number of security threads such as breakout to underlying host OS.

Currently the kube-proxy DaemonSet runs in privileged mode.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/863a462eeccca4c24bf4c4e9012f5ebccade70a2/cluster/addons/kube-proxy/kube-proxy-ds.yaml#L50-L51

https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy describes how to run kube-proxy in "rootless". To my understanding "rootless" != non-privileged mode but this configuration can be also used for running in non-privileged mode. However I see that following issues with it:
1. In the provided kube-proxy component config in https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-in-userns/#configuring-kube-proxy we have to disable certain settins to prevent kube-proxy from ensuring sysctls (which is allowed only in privileged container).

But when I tried to run kube-proxy with the prov
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because kube-proxy requires setting certain sysctls that need privileged container mode, but there was no mechanism to run these privileged operations separately from the main non-privileged kube-proxy process. This forced kube-proxy to run fully privileged or fail when run with lowered privileges, with no way to disable these sysctl settings via configuration.
FIX: Added a new `--init-only` command line flag to `kube-proxy`. Setting the flag makes `kube-proxy` perform its initial configuration that requires privileged mode, and then exit. The `--init-only` mode is intended to be executed in a privileged init container, so that the main container may run with a stricter `securityContext`.
